title: Five groups, five worlds: how fish, frogs, snakes, birds and mammals sense the same place

summary.text: Stand by a pond at dusk in Mysuru. A fish feels a falling insect through ripples on her skin. A python in the reeds finds a warm rat with pits on her lips. A pigeon sees colours you cannot, and a dog follows a smell that is hours old. All of them have a backbone, so all are vertebrates. Yet each group has a different sense that stands out, because senses are tools built for a way of life. In this unit you test your own eyes, skin and ears the way these animals use theirs, and ask whether they all live in the same world.
summary.art: A pond at dusk with five animals around it: a fish under the surface with faint ripple lines reaching her sides, a python on a branch with glowing heat pits on her lips, a pigeon on a wall with a faint rainbow halo around her eyes, a frog on a leaf with a round eardrum, and a dog with a nose lifted into a visible scent trail.

intro.hook: A barn owl sits on a beam in a granary with every light switched off. She hears a rat nibble ragi on the floor, drops silently, and catches him. She never needed to see him. How can an animal hunt well in complete darkness, and what other senses do animals have that we do not?
intro.text: People often say there are five senses: sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch. Animals with a backbone have those, and more. A fish has a line of tiny sensors along her sides that feel water move. Some snakes have pits that feel the heat of a warm body from a distance. Many birds see colours that people cannot see at all. In this unit you will meet the five groups of animals with a backbone again: fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals. This time you ask what each group senses best, and how you can test a little of it with your own body.
intro.art: A dark granary with a barn owl on a beam, her heart-shaped face turned towards a small rat on the floor, and faint curved sound lines going from the rat to the owl's ears.

outcomes: I can name the five groups of animals with a backbone and say one sense that stands out in each group, with an Indian example.
I can say what a sense organ does: it picks up one kind of signal, such as light, sound, vibration, smell, heat or water movement.
I can explain how a fish feels water move with her lateral line, and how some snakes find warm prey with heat pits.
I can explain why many hunted animals have eyes on the sides of their head and many hunters have eyes at the front.
I can explain how the shape of an ear helps an animal tell where a sound came from.
I can run a fair test on my own senses, record the results in a table, and say what I think, what I saw and why.
I can say that animals sense different parts of the same place, give one sense an animal has that I do not, and name something scientists still do not know about animal senses.

terms.meaning: A part of the body, such as an eye, an ear or a nose, that picks up one kind of signal from the world.
terms.example: Your nose is the sense organ for smell.
terms.art: A child's face with arrows pointing from the eyes, ears, nose and tongue to small labels.

terms.meaning: A tiny cell inside a sense organ that reacts to one kind of signal, such as light, a smell or a push, and sends a message on.
terms.example: The receptors in your eye react to light.
terms.art: A magnified picture of a few cells in an eye, with small arrows of light going in and a thin line going out.

terms.meaning: Anything in the world that a sense can pick up, such as light, sound, heat, a smell or a ripple.
terms.example: A ripple on the water is a signal for a fish.
terms.art: A pond with small icons floating above it: a sun ray, a sound wave, a flame, a scent cloud and a ripple.

terms.meaning: A line of tiny sensors along the sides of a fish. They feel water moving past the body.
terms.example: A fish in muddy water uses her lateral line to feel where another fish is.
terms.art: A silver fish with a dotted line along her side, and ripple rings arriving from a falling insect.

terms.meaning: A thin, tight skin that shakes when sound reaches it. The shaking is passed to the inner ear.
terms.example: A frog has a round eardrum on each side of the head, with no ear flap.
terms.art: A green frog on a leaf with a bright round disc behind each eye, circled.

terms.meaning: The part of the ear that sticks out from the head and collects sound. Its scientific name is the pinna.
terms.example: A fox turns her large ear flaps towards a sound.
terms.art: A fox with big upright ears turned towards faint sound lines drawn in the air.

terms.meaning: A small hollow in the face of some snakes that feels the heat given off by warm bodies.
terms.example: An Indian rock python has rows of heat pits along her lips.
terms.art: A close-up of a python's head with small pits along the lips and faint orange glow lines from a warm rat.

terms.meaning: Heat that travels as invisible rays from a warm body. People cannot see it, but skin can feel it.
terms.example: You feel infrared on your face when you stand near a lit diya.
terms.art: A lit diya with faint wavy orange lines reaching a child's cheek.

terms.meaning: A kind of light that people cannot see. Many birds can see it.
terms.example: A bird may see a pattern in a flower or feather that is only in ultraviolet.
terms.art: A pigeon feather shown twice: plain for human eyes, and with a bright glowing pattern as a bird would see it.

terms.meaning: A cell in the eye that senses colour. Different cones react to different colours.
terms.example: People have three kinds of cones, and many birds have four.
terms.art: A diagram of an eye with three small cones in red, green and blue beside four cones in a bird's eye.

terms.meaning: How much of the space around you your eyes can see at one time, measured in degrees.
terms.example: A pigeon sees almost all the way round. An owl sees only a narrow slice in front.
terms.art: A top view of a pigeon and an owl, each with a coloured wedge showing how far around they see.

terms.meaning: Seeing the same thing with two eyes at once. It lets the brain judge how far away something is.
terms.example: A cat uses both eyes to judge a jump onto a wall.
terms.art: A cat's face from above with two overlapping cones of sight meeting on a mouse.

terms.meaning: Finding things by making a sound and listening to the echo that bounces back.
terms.example: A small bat calls out in the dark and hears the echo from a flying moth.
terms.art: A bat in flight with sound arcs going out to a moth and echo arcs coming back.

terms.meaning: Very low sound that people cannot hear, though they may feel it as a throb.
terms.example: Asian elephants call to each other with infrasound across a forest.
terms.art: Two elephants far apart with long slow sound waves moving between them through trees.

terms.meaning: An animal that other animals hunt and eat.
terms.example: A rat is prey for a barn owl.
terms.art: A small rat on a granary floor looking up warily.

terms.meaning: An animal that hunts and eats other animals.
terms.example: A barn owl is a predator of rats.
terms.art: A barn owl gliding down towards the floor with open talons.

explanations.concept: What a sense is: a way to pick up one kind of signal
explanations.definition: A sense is a way a body picks up one kind of signal. Tiny cells called receptors react to the signal and send a message to the brain. Receptors are often gathered in a sense organ, such as an eye or an ear.
explanations.description: The world is full of signals. There is light, sound, smell, heat, touch and the movement of water or air. No receptor reacts to all of them. An eye reacts to light but not to smell. A nose reacts to tiny bits of a thing but not to sound. So every sense is a kind of question. The eye asks, where is the light? The ear asks, where is the shaking? All animals with a backbone have eyes, ears, a nose, taste and touch. But the five groups have developed some senses much further than others, and a few groups have senses that people do not have at all.
examples: A cat's whiskers react to a push from air or a wall.
A frog's eardrum reacts to the shaking of sound.
A fish's lateral line reacts to moving water.
explanations.art: Five small panels showing a signal, a receptor and a brain for light, sound, smell, heat and water movement.

explanations.concept: Fish: feeling water move with the lateral line
explanations.definition: A lateral line is a row of tiny sensors along a fish's head and sides. Each sensor has a bundle of hairs that bends when water moves past. The bending sends a message to the brain.
explanations.description: Water is thick, and it carries movement a long way. When another fish swims past, or an insect lands on the surface, the water moves. A fish with a lateral line feels that movement along her whole body, even in muddy or dark water. She can tell the direction and often how far. Many fish also hear through an inner ear that sits inside the head, with no ear opening. Their bodies are mostly water, so sound goes straight through. Fish smell with nostrils that take in water. Catfish such as magur have whiskers called barbels with taste cells, so they can taste the mud as they feel along it. Sharks and rays can even sense the very weak electricity made by the muscles of other animals.
examples: A rohu or catla in a pond turns towards a ripple without seeing what made it.
A magur catfish tastes the muddy bottom with her whiskers.
A shark can find a fish hidden in sand by the electricity of that fish's muscles.
explanations.art: A cutaway of a fish with the lateral line highlighted along her side and arrows of water movement reaching it.

explanations.concept: Amphibians: eardrums, thin skin and eyes for movement
explanations.definition: A frog has a round eardrum on each side of her head, behind the eye. Sound shakes the eardrum, and the shaking is passed to the inner ear.
explanations.description: A frog has no ear flap. Her eardrum sits flat on the skin, like the skin of a drum. Frogs hear each other's calls, and during the monsoon the calls of male frogs fill the night so that females can find them. A frog's eyes bulge on top of her head, so she can see above the water while most of her body stays hidden. In 1959 a team at MIT in the USA studied a frog's eye and found cells that react to small dark moving things, like flies. This is one reason a frog may ignore a dead fly that lies still, and snap at one that moves. Tadpoles have a lateral line like a fish. Many adult amphibians keep it only if they live in water. Frog skin is thin and wet, and also senses touch and some chemicals.
examples: The loud chorus of Indian bullfrogs in the first monsoon rains.
A frog sits with only her eyes above the water.
Tadpoles feel ripples with a lateral line, and then lose it as they leave the water.
explanations.art: A frog at the edge of a monsoon puddle with only her eyes above the water, a round eardrum circled behind each eye, and a fly moving in front of her.

explanations.concept: Reptiles: scent from the tongue, feeling the ground and sensing heat
explanations.definition: A heat pit is a small hollow on a snake's face with a thin membrane inside. It reacts to the infrared given off by warm bodies. Pit vipers, boas and pythons have them.
explanations.description: A snake has no outer ear and no eardrum on the outside. She feels the shaking of the ground through her jaw bone, and her inner ear picks it up. Her forked tongue flicks out, collects tiny bits of scent from the air and the ground, and wipes them onto two spots in the roof of her mouth. The two tips of the fork can gather scent from two sides at once, which may help her follow a trail. Some snakes can also sense heat. An Indian rock python has rows of small heat pits along her lips. Cobras and Russell's vipers do not have pits. Crocodiles have tiny dark dots on their jaws that feel ripples and pressure, so a mugger crocodile can feel a fish swim near without seeing the fish. Some geckos can see colour in light so dim that people see only grey.
examples: A python senses the heat of a rat in a dark storeroom.
A cobra follows scent with her tongue.
A mugger crocodile floats with her jaws just under the water, ready to feel a ripple.
explanations.art: A python's head from the side, with heat pits along the lip, forked tongue out, and a warm rat shown as an orange glow in the dark.

explanations.concept: Birds: sharp eyes, extra colours and hearing
explanations.definition: Most birds have four kinds of colour cones in their eyes. People have three. The fourth kind lets a bird see ultraviolet light.
explanations.description: Sight is the main sense for most birds. Their eyes are large for the size of their head, and they see small details and fast movement very well. Because of the fourth cone, a bird sees colours and patterns that we do not. In 2005 a scientist named Mark Eaton checked the feathers of many birds. He found that in most species where males and females look the same to us, the two sexes look different in ultraviolet. Birds also hear well. A barn owl has a flat, heart-shaped face that works like a dish and gathers sound, and her two ears sit at slightly different heights. She can catch a mouse in a completely dark room by sound alone. Most birds do not smell strongly, but a few do. A turkey vulture can find food by smell.
examples: A male and a female of many bird kinds look alike to us, but look different to each other in ultraviolet.
A barn owl catches a rat in a dark granary by sound.
A crow notices a small movement on the road from far away.
explanations.art: A male and a female bird that look alike, shown twice: plain as people see them, and with different glowing patterns as other birds of their kind see them in ultraviolet.

explanations.concept: Mammals: smell, ears and whiskers, and sounds we cannot hear
explanations.definition: Mammals are the only animals with three tiny bones in the middle ear, which pass sound from the eardrum to the inner ear. Most mammals also have ear flaps that can collect sound.
explanations.description: Many mammals live by smell. A dog has many tens of times more smell receptors in her nose than a person has, and the part of her brain for smell is large. A cat or a deer turns her ear flaps one at a time towards a sound. Whiskers are long, stiff hairs with a rich supply of nerves at the base. They feel a push from air or from a wall in the dark. Harbour seals can follow the swirl left in the water by a fish that swam past about half a minute ago, using only their whiskers. Small insect-eating bats such as the Indian pipistrelle make sounds too high for people to hear, then listen to the echoes. In 1984 Katy Payne stood near elephants at a zoo in Oregon in the USA and felt a throbbing in the air that she could not hear. She later recorded Asian elephants calling with sounds too low for people to hear. Elephants also feel rumbles through the ground with their feet.
examples: A dog follows the smell of someone who walked past an hour ago.
A bat finds a moth by the echo of her own call.
An elephant listens to a far-off call through her feet and trunk.
explanations.art: A dog sniffing a trail, a fox with turned ear flaps, a bat sending sound and hearing an echo, and an elephant with her foot on the ground and long slow sound waves.

explanations.concept: Wide view or deep view: where the eyes sit
explanations.definition: A field of view is how much space around you your eyes can see at once. Binocular vision is when both eyes see the same space, which helps judge how far away something is.
explanations.description: Eyes on the sides of the head see a very wide view. A pigeon sees about 340 degrees, almost all the way round. A horse also sees almost all the way round. That is useful to an animal that is hunted, because she can spot a hunter coming from almost any side. But the two eyes share very little space, so she does not judge distance well with both eyes together. Eyes at the front of the head, as in a person or an owl, see a narrower view, but the two eyes overlap in a large area. The brain compares the two pictures and works out how far away something is. That helps a hunter pounce, or an animal jump from branch to branch. A person sees about 200 degrees in total, and an owl somewhere near 110 degrees, because books give slightly different numbers. An owl cannot move her eyes in their sockets, so she turns her whole head, up to about 270 degrees.
examples: A pigeon on a wall notices a cat creeping up from behind.
A cat judges the distance to a mouse before she jumps.
A person catching a ball with one eye closed finds it much harder.
explanations.art: Top view of a pigeon with a very wide coloured wedge and a small overlap, beside a barn owl with a narrow wedge and a big overlap.

explanations.concept: Colour: who sees more, and who sees less
explanations.definition: Colour vision depends on how many kinds of cone an animal has. More kinds of cone usually means more colours can be told apart.
explanations.description: People have three kinds of cones, so we see red, green, blue and everything mixed from them. Most mammals have only two kinds. A dog is not colour-blind in the sense of seeing only black and white. A dog sees blues and yellows well, but cannot tell red from green, like some people. Many birds, fish, turtles and some lizards have four kinds, including one for ultraviolet. A goldfish can see ultraviolet light. So the same pond looks different to a dog, a person and a bird. Seeing more colours is not always better. Animals that hunt at night usually trade colour for the ability to see in dim light.
examples: A dog sees a red ball on green grass as a dull ball on yellowish grass.
A pigeon tells apart colours that look the same to us.
A gecko at night has to see in dim light.
explanations.art: The same garden scene drawn three ways: as a person sees it, as a dog sees it with blue and yellow only, and as a bird sees it with extra bright patterns.

explanations.concept: Senses people do not have: electric, heat and magnetic
explanations.description: Some animals sense signals that people cannot sense at all. Sharks and rays feel the electricity that other animals' muscles make. Some snakes feel infrared heat. Many birds, turtles and fish seem to use the Earth's magnetic field to find their way. Scientists have shown this by changing the magnetic field around the animals and seeing them change direction. How the animals sense the field is still debated. Nobody has found the magnetic receptor with certainty. This is one of the open puzzles in biology.
examples: A shark finds a fish hidden under sand by the weak electricity the fish gives off.
A python feels the heat of a rat in the dark.
A migrating bird holds her course on a cloudy night.
explanations.art: A shark with faint electric field lines, a python with heat glow, and a bird with Earth's magnetic field lines curving from pole to pole.

perspectives.explanation: A protein in the eye, called cryptochrome, may react to the magnetic field when light hits it. Birds might then see the field as a pattern laid over what they see. Robins stopped finding their way when weak radio noise disturbed this effect.

Tiny pieces of the iron mineral magnetite in the body may act like a small compass needle. Cells with iron were once found in birds' beaks, but later work showed that many of them were white blood cells, not nerve cells.
Some scientists think an animal might use one method for the compass direction and another for a map of where she is. Nobody knows yet.

explanations.description: Eyes, ears and the brain parts that read them use a lot of energy. A body that spends energy on a sense it hardly needs wastes food. Mexican tetras that live in dark caves have lost their eyes, and a study in 2015 worked out that keeping eyes would cost them a noticeable part of their daily energy. They have more sensors on their lateral lines instead. The Ganges river dolphin, called susu, lives in muddy water where eyes are little help. Her eyes have no working lens and tell only light from dark. She finds fish by sending out clicks and listening for the echoes. The Ganges river dolphin is India's national aquatic animal. So each animal's senses are a trade, and they fit the place where her body lives. This is an idea that most biologists accept, but the exact costs are still being measured.
examples: A cave fish with no eyes and a strong lateral line.
A susu in the muddy Ganges, finding fish by echoes.
A deer in the dark who hears and smells more than she sees.
explanations.art: A blind cave fish with a strongly marked lateral line, beside a Ganges river dolphin sending clicks in brown water.

explanations.description: Put a fish, a pigeon, a snake and a person at the same pond. They have different senses, so they notice different things. The question is what this means. The German biologist Jakob von Uexküll wrote in 1934 that each animal lives in her own sensory world, which he called an umwelt. His famous example was a tick. A tick waits on a branch and reacts to three signals only: the smell of sweat acid, warmth of about body heat, and the touch of hairy skin. Nothing else about the world matters to her. Other scientists say there is just one world, and each animal gets a partial view of that world, as if looking through different windows. Which is it? We can compare what animals sense, but we cannot yet say what it is like to sense as a bat does.
examples: A dog that smells a whole story on a lamp post, while a person smells nothing.
A bird that sees a feather pattern in ultraviolet that a person never sees.
A tick that responds to only three things in the whole world.
explanations.art: One pond drawn in four ways, as a person, a fish, a snake and a bird might sense it: ordinary colours, ripples, heat glow and extra bright patterns.

perspectives.explanation: Each animal lives inside her own sensory world, made of the signals her body can pick up and the things that matter to her. A tick and a person really do live in different worlds.

There is one real world. Every animal senses a part of it, like different windows onto one room. We can learn the rest of the room by using instruments, and by comparing what different animals notice.

agreed.text: All animals with a backbone sense light, sound or shaking, smell and taste, touch and balance. The five groups have developed some of these senses much further than others.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have looked inside the bodies of fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals, and recorded messages from their nerves when each kind of signal is given.

agreed.text: Fish feel moving water with the lateral line.
agreed.evidence: When scientists switch off the lateral line with a mild chemical, fish find the source of a ripple much less well in the dark, while fish with a working lateral line find it easily.

agreed.text: Some snakes sense the heat of warm bodies with heat pits.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have blindfolded pit vipers such as rattlesnakes. The snakes still struck at a warm target, and did not strike at a cool one.

agreed.text: A barn owl can find a mouse in total darkness using only sound.
agreed.evidence: In 1971 Roger Payne tested barn owls in a pitch-dark room. They landed on a rustling piece of paper pulled across the floor. This also worked when there was no mouse, only the paper.

agreed.text: Many bats find their way and their food by echolocation.
agreed.evidence: In 1938 Donald Griffin and Robert Galambos used a microphone that could pick up very high sounds. They recorded bats calling, and showed that bats with their mouths taped shut crashed into obstacles.

agreed.text: Most birds have four kinds of colour cone in their eyes, and can see ultraviolet light.
agreed.evidence: The cones of many birds have been studied under the microscope, and birds respond in tests to patterns that exist only in ultraviolet.

challenging.who: A very old saying, 'blind as a bat'.
challenging.for: Bats fly easily in the dark, and many small bats use sound more than sight.
challenging.against: All bats can see. Large fruit bats, such as the Indian flying fox, find ripe fruit with their eyes and their noses. Small bats that use echolocation can also see.

challenging.claim: A snake stings with her tongue.
challenging.who: Many people, because the tongue flicks like a tiny stinger.
challenging.for: The forked tongue moves fast and looks sharp.
challenging.against: The tongue is soft and harmless. It carries tiny bits of scent into the mouth. A snake bites with her teeth, and some snakes use fangs to put venom in.

challenging.claim: Dogs see only in black and white.
challenging.who: A popular belief in many places.
challenging.for: Dogs do not seem to care about colour, and their eyes have fewer colour cones than ours.
challenging.against: Dogs can tell blue from yellow. They have two kinds of cones. What they cannot do is tell red from green, like some people.

challenging.claim: An owl can turn her head all the way round.
challenging.for: An owl turns her head so far that she can look straight behind her.
challenging.against: An owl turns her head about 270 degrees, three-quarters of the way round. She has extra neck bones and special blood vessels that let her do this without cutting off blood to her brain.

challenging.claim: A frog will starve beside a pile of dead flies, because she cannot see food that does not move.
challenging.who: A claim often made after the 1959 frog eye study.
challenging.for: A frog's eye has cells that react most to small moving dark things, and a frog in a bare tank may ignore still food.
challenging.against: A frog also uses smell, and some frogs learn to eat still food in captivity, especially if it is wiggled. The study showed what the eye reports, not everything a frog does.

challenging.claim: Birds sense the Earth's magnetic field through their eyes.
challenging.who: Some biologists, such as Thorsten Ritz and Klaus Schulten, and many later researchers.
challenging.for: Robins lose their direction when weak radio noise disturbs a chemical effect in the eye, and the effect needs light.
challenging.against: No one has found the receptor with certainty, and some experiments point to iron-based sensors or to more than one method.

big_questions.q: A python senses a rat as a warm glow. A person senses the same rat as a shape and a smell. Which of them is sensing what the rat really is?
big_questions.hint: Think about whether 'warm', 'brown' and 'smelly' belong to the rat, or to the meeting of a rat and a body.

big_questions.q: Hunted animals tend to have eyes on the sides of the head, and hunters have eyes at the front. What does each way of seeing gain, and what does it lose?
big_questions.hint: Think about the wide view and the deep view that you tested.

big_questions.q: A lateral line works well in water but would work badly in air. Why?
big_questions.hint: Think about how far a ripple travels in water, and how far a puff of air moves a feather.

big_questions.q: The philosopher Thomas Nagel asked in 1974, 'What is it like to be a bat?' Could you ever find out? What would count as an answer?
big_questions.hint: A bat can hear echoes, and you can only imagine them. Is imagining enough?

big_questions.q: Cameras can record ultraviolet and heat that we cannot see. Do such cameras show the world as it really is?
big_questions.hint: A camera also picks up only some signals. Who chooses which ones?

big_questions.q: If you could borrow one sense from another animal for a day, which one would you pick, and what do you think you would find out?
big_questions.hint: Think about a place you know well, such as your street, and what might be hiding in it.

big_questions.q: An owl turns her head, a deer turns her ears and a snake flicks her tongue. In each case, what is the animal doing, and what question is she asking the world?
big_questions.hint: Each movement points a sense organ at a place. Notice which sense it is.

big_questions.q: Dogs can be trained to sniff out some illnesses in people. What does that tell you about what a smell can carry?
big_questions.hint: A smell is made of tiny bits of a thing. What else might be carried in those bits?

story.title: The Owl in the Granary
story.note: A made-up story. Kavya, Ajji and Farhan are imagined, though Mandya, in Karnataka, is a real place where ragi is grown. The science is real: barn owls hunt by sound, even in a pitch-dark room, as Roger Payne showed in 1971. Owl pellets really do hold the fur and bones of what the owl ate. In some places people believe that an owl in the house is a bad sign. In others the owl is a friend of the farmer.
text: In the holidays, Kavya went to her grandmother's house near Mandya. Her cousin Farhan came from Hyderabad. It was the time after the ragi harvest, and the sacks stood in the store room behind the house, piled up to the beam.
Every morning, Ajji came out of the store room with her lips tight. 'The rats were here again,' she said. A sack in the corner had a hole, and a small heap of ragi lay on the floor like brown sand.

Ajji had her own plan. At night she left an oil lamp burning in the store room, because rats hate light. When she heard a rustle, she banged a steel plate with a spoon. The noise was so loud that the whole house jumped. The rats ran. But in the morning there was always another hole.

High on the beam above the sacks lived a white barn owl. She had a pale heart-shaped face and big dark eyes. Ajji did not like her at all. 'An owl in the house brings bad luck,' she said. 'My own grandmother told me so.' She waved a broom at the beam every evening. The owl only looked down at her, blinked, and sat still.

One morning, Kavya found grey lumps on the floor under the beam. They were as big as her thumb and dry like old felt. 'Dirt,' said Farhan. Kavya was not so sure. She pulled one apart with a stick, and inside she found fur, and then thin white bones. At the very end she found a tiny skull with two long front teeth. 'This is a rat,' she said slowly. 'The owl eats them. Ajji, she is working for you.'

Ajji sniffed. 'She may eat one now and then,' she said. 'But the rats come back every night.' Kavya thought about this all day. At night the lamp was burning and the plate was banging, so the owl could not be hunting. Maybe that was the problem.

'How does she catch them at all?' asked Farhan. 'It is pitch dark under the beam, except for the lamp.' 'With her eyes,' said Kavya. 'Owls have night eyes.' But then she stopped. 'If she can see in the dark, why does Ajji put a lamp?' And then she asked a better question. 'What if she does not need to see?'

The next evening, Kavya asked Ajji to put out the lamp. Ajji frowned for a long time. Then she agreed, as long as she herself would sit in the doorway with them. They sat on a mat, all three, with the door open only a hand-width. The store room was black. Kavya could not see her own fingers.

For a long time nothing happened. The wind moved in the coconut trees outside. Then there was a tiny sound, a dry scratch, like a fingernail on paper. A rat was working at a sack. Almost at once there was a soft whoosh of air, and then a squeak, and then nothing. Farhan snapped on his torch. The beam was empty. The owl was already back on her perch, with something in her claws.
'She did not even need the torch,' whispered Farhan. 'She did not need a lamp either,' said Kavya. 'She heard him.' Ajji said nothing, but she was staring up at the beam.

Kavya wanted to be sure. The next night, she tied a cloth bag to the end of a long string. She filled it with a handful of dry husks, so it would make a dry little rustle. She laid it in the far corner, and held the other end of the string at the doorway. The room was dark again. Ajji sat beside her. Nobody spoke.

Kavya gave the string one small pull. The husks whispered. Up on the beam, there was a tiny movement. Kavya pulled again. Then the white shape slid off the beam without a sound, and dropped. She landed right on the bag, and pinned it with her claws. Kavya heard her stand very still, as if waiting for the bag to move. It did not. There was no rat there, only husks and a cloth.

Farhan laughed out loud, so quietly that it was almost just air. The owl flew back to the beam. Ajji let out a long breath. 'She went for the sound,' she said. 'She never saw it.' 'And she turned her whole face to the sound before she dropped,' said Kavya. 'Her face is like a dish. It catches the sound and sends it to her ears.'

Ajji sat for a while in the dark. Then she said, 'My grandmother was a wise woman. But she did not sit in the dark and pull a string.' She said it gently, and Kavya did not laugh. 'Each of us sees what we see,' said Ajji. 'Tonight I have seen something new.'

That night, Ajji blew out the lamp for good. She opened the little window under the roof, so the owl could come and go. She put the steel plate back in the kitchen, where it belonged. A week later, the sacks were whole. A fortnight later, there were no new holes at all, only grey pellets on the floor, which Farhan swept up every morning with great seriousness.

On the last night of the holidays, Kavya sat on the mat and pressed both hands behind her ears, with her fingers pointing forward. The rustle of a leaf in the yard suddenly sounded bigger and closer. She took her hands away, and it shrank again. 'So that is why foxes have big ears,' she whispered. Up on the beam, the owl turned her face and looked at her.
story.epiphany: An owl does not need light to find a rat. She hears the rustle, turns her dish-shaped face towards it, and drops. In the dark, a lamp helps the rats more than it helps the owl.
ask: A barn owl in a dark room drops onto a rustling bag that has no rat in it. What does that tell you about how she finds prey?
Why might loud banging near a barn owl make it harder for her to catch a rat, even if it makes the rats run?
If you cup your hands behind your ears, a faint rustle sounds louder. What do your hands do, and which animals have ears that do the same job?

Kavya on her knees with a stick, pulling apart a grey owl pellet, and a tiny rat skull showing inside it.

how_we_found_out.story: In 1793 an Italian priest and scientist named Lazzaro Spallanzani wanted to know how bats fly in the dark without hitting anything. People then believed that eyes were the only way to find a path through a room. So he covered the eyes of bats, and they flew around the room and avoided obstacles just as before. Next he blocked their ears, and the bats bumped into things. He concluded that the ears were doing the work of eyes. A famous French scientist, Georges Cuvier, did not believe it. He said that bats must feel the air with the skin of their wings. For nearly 150 years nobody could prove who was right. Then in 1938 two students, Donald Griffin and Robert Galambos, used a new microphone that could pick up very high sounds. It showed that bats make sounds too high for people to hear, and listen for the echoes.
how_we_found_out.who: Lazzaro Spallanzani, Georges Cuvier, Donald Griffin and Robert Galambos
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That eyes are the only way to find a path in the dark, so bats must be feeling the air with their skin.

roots.context: We have seen that a fish, a snake, a bird and a bat each sense a different slice of the same place. Now we ask what that tells us about the world and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: A fish feels the pond as moving water. A python feels it as warm and cool. A pigeon sees colours we never see. So the world each of us notices is only the slice our body was built to catch.
deep_truth.habit: We say 'the dark', 'the pond' or 'the colour of the feather' as if every animal met the same picture. But the dark is not dark to an owl who hears, and a feather has a pattern for birds that people never see.
deep_truth.evidence: In the wide-view test, most people see a little more than half the way round, while a pigeon sees almost all the way round. In the ripple test, most people feel a ripple only when it is close, while a fish feels one along her whole side. An owl catches a rat in a pitch-dark granary by sound alone.

three.who_am_i: You are one animal among many, and your eyes, ears and skin show you only a slice of what is there.
three.what_is_life: Every living being, from a tick to an elephant, listens to the world in her own way, and answers it.
three.what_is_this_world: It looks like one place that many bodies sense in many ways, and no body senses all of it.

roots.thread: All animals with a backbone began as small fish in the sea more than 500 million years ago. Each group kept its own senses and grew some of them very far. Yet all senses do one job. They let something in the world reach a body, and let the body answer. Every sense organ is a place where one part of nature picks up a signal from another part.

teachings.teaching: The Upanishad speaks of the ear of the ear, the mind of the mind, the speech of speech and the eye of the eye. It points to something behind each sense that does the sensing.
teachings.link: A fish, a bat and a bird all hear, feel and see in different ways. The teaching asks what is the same behind all those different ears and eyes.

teachings.source: Udana 6.4, the blind men and the elephant
teachings.teaching: In this old story from the Buddhist teachings, several blind men each touch a different part of an elephant. One feels a leg, another the tail, another an ear. Each describes a different animal, and each argues that he is right.
teachings.link: Each group of animals senses a different part of the same place. No body gets the whole elephant, and each is partly right.

teachings.teaching: Two friends stand on a bridge over a river. Zhuangzi says the fish are happy. His friend Huizi says, you are not a fish, so how do you know? Zhuangzi answers, you are not me, so how do you know that I do not know?
teachings.link: We cannot sense a lateral line or a heat pit from the inside. The old question remains: how far can one being know what it is like to be another?

science.text: Each animal can pick up only some of the signals around her, and the signals differ from group to group. The biologist Jakob von Uexküll called each animal's sensory world her umwelt.
Nobody knows what it feels like to sense as a bat or a snake does. In 1974 the philosopher Thomas Nagel asked 'What is it like to be a bat?' to show how hard the question is.

other_view.view: A sense is a set of cells that react to a signal and pass it on. What matters is what the animal does with the signal. Asking what the bat feels adds nothing we can test, and may not be a good question.

practice.title: Listen like an owl
practice.say: Sit still and close your eyes. Cup both hands behind your ears, with your fingers pointing forward. Listen for one minute. Count how many sounds you can find, and point to where each one comes from. Now take your hands away and listen again. Then open your eyes and look for each sound.
practice.kid: Sit still. Close your eyes. Cup your hands behind your ears. Listen for one minute. How many sounds can you find? Point to each. Then open your eyes.

ask: If a pigeon could look at your street, what would she say you are missing?
A python senses a rat as a warm glow. Is the rat warm, or bright, or smelly? Who decides?
Is there a sense that no animal has found yet?
When you and a dog smell the same lamp post, are you smelling the same thing?
roots.art: A pond at dusk drawn as one picture split into five strips, each strip showing how a fish, a frog, a python, a pigeon and a dog might sense it, with a child standing at the edge looking at all five.

experiments.title: Wide View, Deep View: how far round can you see, and can you judge distance?
experiments.question: How far round can you see with two eyes, and with only one? And do two eyes help you judge how far away something is?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess two things. At which clock number will you first see the moving card as it comes round from behind you? And will you touch the pen top more often with two eyes or with one? Give a reason for each guess. Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The same person keeps their eyes on the same note on the wall every time, and the same helper waves the same card at the same height and speed. The circle, the chair and the distances do not change. Only the eye that is open changes. Each wide-view test is done twice, because one try can be a fluke. The pen test is done six times for each eye setting, with the pen in a new spot each time.

materials.item: a chair, and a sticky note or small paper stuck on a wall at your child's eye height (use tape or a little paste if there is no sticky note)
7 paper cups or chappals, marked 12, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 on slips of paper
a bright red card or red paper, the size of your hand, taped to a ruler or a stick
a clean cloth or a folded handkerchief to cover one eye
a pen with its cap on, and a lump of clay or atta dough, or a small cup, to stand it in
a table, a ruler, a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: Use a pen with its cap on, never a sharp pencil, and keep it at arm's length from the face so nobody pokes an eye. Cover an eye with a cloth held gently or with the palm. Never press on the eye.
experiments.record: Write down the clock number where your child first saw the card move, for each test. Multiply by 30 to get degrees. For the pen test, count how many times out of 6 the finger touched the cap with two eyes, and with one eye. Draw a bar chart of the best angle for each test, and a second bar chart of the pen hits.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you find out how far round you can see with two eyes and with one eye, and how well two eyes judge distance. Then you compare your eyes with a pigeon's and an owl's.

setup.art: A chair in the middle of a floor with seven cups in a half circle on the right side, numbered 12 to 6 like a clock, and a sticky note on the wall straight ahead.
setup.caption: 1. Set up the chair, the note and the seven markers like a clock face.

setup.art: A child on the chair looking at the wall note, while a helper behind the child at the number 4 cup waves a red card at eye height.
setup.caption: 2. The child looks at the note. The helper waves the card and moves round the circle.

setup.art: The same child with one eye covered by a hand, and the helper at the number 2 cup waving the card.
setup.caption: 3. Cover one eye and test again.

setup.art: A child at a table with one finger beside her ear, about to touch the cap of a pen standing in clay at arm's length.
setup.caption: 4. Touch the pen cap in one smooth move, first with two eyes.

setup.art: The same child with one eye covered, reaching towards a pen cap and missing it by a little.
setup.caption: 5. Do it again with one eye covered, and count how many times you touch the cap.

flow.do: Show your child the setup. Ask for their two guesses and the reasons. Write them at the top of the results table.
flow.say: Today we test your eyes. A card will come round from behind you, and you say when you first see it move. Then you try to touch a pen with one finger. What do you think will happen, and why do you think so?
flow.kid: We test your eyes today. Guess first. When will you see the card move? Will one eye see less? Why?

ask.q: Why might covering one eye change what you can see?
good: One eye sees less.
The nose gets in the way.
Each eye sees a different side.

flow.parent: Do not correct any guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. One child with a parent: the parent is the helper and the recorder. Two to four children: one sits, one waves the card, one writes the numbers, and the others watch silently and then swap. Everyone gets their own row in the results table, so write each child's name on it. Only one child sits and is tested at a time.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Wide View, Deep View test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Put the chair in the middle of an open floor. Stick the note on the wall 2 metres straight ahead, at your child's eye height. Put the 7 markers in a half circle on the right side, 1 metre from the chair. Number 12 is straight ahead, 3 is straight to the right, and 6 is right behind.
flow.say: Sit here and look at the note on the wall. Keep your head still. The numbers on the floor are like a clock. Twelve is in front of you, three is on your right, and six is right behind you.
flow.kid: Sit on the chair. Look at the note on the wall. Keep your head still.
flow.parent: Paper cups or chappals make good markers. Put each number on a slip under its marker. The helper will stand beside each marker and hold the card at your child's eye height.

check.q: Why must your child keep looking at the note on the wall?
options: So only the card moves, and the eyes stay still
So the child does not get bored
So the card is easier to see
check.why: If the eyes turn towards the card, the test measures how far you can turn your eyes. It does not measure how far round you can see. Looking at one fixed point keeps the test fair.

flow.context: In this step, you set up a clock circle on the floor, so you can measure how far round you can see.

flow.do: Test with both eyes open. The helper starts at marker 6, behind the chair, and holds the card at eye height. The helper waves the card gently up and down for 3 seconds. Then the helper moves to marker 5, waves again, and so on. The child says 'now' when they first see anything move. Write down the number. Do the whole test twice.
flow.say: I will wave the card behind you, then move round the circle. Say now, the moment you see anything move, even a blur. Keep looking at the note.
flow.kid: Look at the note. Say now when you see the card move.

ask.q: At which number did you first see it move? Could you see its colour straight away?
good: Around three or four.
I saw something move, but not what it was.
The colour came later.

flow.parent: Most people first notice movement around 3 or 4 on the clock, which is 90 to 120 degrees from straight ahead. Colour usually comes later, nearer the front. Your child's numbers may differ. Write down what you get.
flow.context: In this step, you find the clock number where your child first sees the card move, with both eyes open.

flow.do: Ask your child to cover the left eye with the cloth. They keep looking at the note with the right eye. Test the right side twice, as before. Then they cover the right eye and you test the right side twice again. Write down each number.
flow.say: Cover your left eye gently. The card comes round on your right side again. Say now when you see it move. Then we cover the right eye and do it again.
flow.kid: Cover one eye. Say now when the card moves. Then swap eyes.

ask.q: With which eye covered did you see the card latest? Why do you think that happened?
good: With my right eye covered.
My nose was in the way.
The right eye looks out to the right.

flow.parent: With the right eye covered, the nose blocks the view on the right, so the card usually shows up much later, around 1 or 2. With the left eye covered, the right eye still sees almost as far as with both eyes. Hold the cloth or palm lightly in front of the eye and never press on the eye.

check.q: The card comes in from the right. Which eye can see it earliest?
options: The right eye, because it looks out to the right
The left eye, because it is stronger
Both eyes see it at the same moment
check.why: The right eye sits on the right side of the face and looks out to the right. The left eye has the nose in the way. Picking the left eye usually means thinking that one eye is better than the other, when in fact it is the side that matters.

flow.context: In this step, you repeat the card test with one eye covered, to see how far round each eye sees.

flow.do: Turn each clock number into degrees by multiplying by 30. Write the angle in the last column. Then double the best angle for both open eyes. This is a rough size of the whole view.
flow.say: Twelve is zero degrees, straight ahead. Each number is 30 degrees more. If you saw it at four, that is four times thirty, which is 120 degrees. What angle did you get with both eyes open?
flow.kid: Multiply the clock number by 30. That is the angle. Write it down.
flow.parent: The doubled number assumes the left side sees as far as the right. For most people it comes out between about 180 and 240 degrees in total. Do not worry if the number is different. Small angles in this test are normal because the card is small and slow.
flow.context: In this step, you turn clock numbers into angles, so you can compare your view with other animals.

flow.do: Sit your child at a table. Stand the capped pen in clay on the table, about 40 centimetres in front of them. Your child holds one finger beside their ear. They swing the finger down and touch the cap in one smooth move. They must not feel for it. Do six tries with both eyes open. After each try, move the pen to a new spot 30, 40 or 50 centimetres away. Count how many touches.
flow.say: Hold one finger beside your ear. Look at the pen. Now swing your finger down and touch the top of the cap in one move. No feeling about. I will move the pen after each try.
flow.kid: Hold a finger by your ear. Touch the pen cap in one move.
flow.parent: A touch means the fingertip lands on the cap. A near miss counts as a miss. Move the pen to a new place each time so your child cannot predict where it will be. Start the card test with one eye on some children and with both eyes on others, and do the pen test with one eye first for the next child. Practice makes the second set a little better, and swapping the order keeps it fair. Six tries is few, so a difference of one touch means little. A difference of three or more is a real sign.
flow.context: In this step, you test how well you judge distance with both eyes open.

flow.do: Now your child covers one eye. Do six more tries with the pen in new spots. Count how many touches. Compare the two counts.
flow.say: Cover one eye gently. Look at the pen with the other eye. Touch the top of the cap in one move, like before.
flow.kid: Cover one eye. Touch the pen cap in one move.

check.q: A child touches the cap 5 times out of 6 with two eyes, and 2 times out of 6 with one eye. What does this suggest?
options: Two eyes help to judge distance
One eye is better than two
The pen moved by itself
check.why: Each eye sees the pen from a slightly different place. The brain compares the two pictures and works out how far away it is. With one eye that comparison is missing, so it is harder to judge distance. Picking 'one eye is better' goes against the counts.

flow.parent: Most people touch the cap more often with two eyes. Your child's counts may be different, and that is fine. If one eye does as well as two, say so honestly. Some people judge distance well with one eye by using other clues, such as size.
flow.context: In this step, you do the pen test again with one eye covered, and compare.

flow.do: Draw one bar chart of the best angle for each wide-view test. Draw a second bar chart of the pen touches. Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why. Then tell them: a pigeon sees about 340 degrees, and an owl about 110 degrees.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened? Now look at the numbers. A pigeon sees about 340 degrees, and an owl about 110. These are typical figures, and books differ. Which one needs to see behind, and which one needs to judge distance?
flow.kid: Draw the bars. Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.
flow.think: A pigeon is hunted and an owl hunts. How do their eyes fit that?
flow.parent: A strong answer says something like this: eyes on the sides see a wider view, and eyes at the front overlap and judge distance. If your child says the nose got in the way, that is a very good observation. Do not explain until they have said what they saw.
flow.context: In this step, you draw your results and compare your eyes with a pigeon's and an owl's.

experiments.title: Ripple Skin: how far away can your hands feel a ripple?
experiments.question: A fish feels a ripple with her lateral line. How far away can your hands feel a ripple, and can you tell which side it came from?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Your hands are in still water and a ripple starts to your left or right. Will you tell the side correctly when it is close? Will you at 20 centimetres? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The same helper makes every ripple with the same gentle dip of one fingertip. The water is still before each ripple. Your child's ears are covered, so only the skin can sense it. A coin toss decides left or right, so the helper cannot make a pattern. Only the distance changes. Each distance is tried 10 times, because one try can be a fluke.
results_table: Score you would get by pure guessing

materials.item: a wide basin or tub at least 60 centimetres long, such as a big steel parat or a baby bath, with about 4 centimetres of still water (cool tap water is fine)
a big towel to put under the basin, and a second towel for the floor
a scarf for closing the eyes, and ear muffs, or a woollen cap or second thick scarf pulled down over the ears
a strip of thin card or a ruler, with marks at 5, 10 and 20 centimetres
a coin
the results table and a pencil

experiments.safety: Put the basin on a towel on a flat, low surface so it does not tip. Wipe up spills at once, because a wet floor is slippery. Keep electrical things, including headphones, away from the water. Cover the ears with ear muffs or a thick cap or scarf, and make sure the child can still breathe and sit comfortably.
experiments.record: For each distance, write how many of the 10 ripples your child located correctly. Guessing alone would give about 5 on average, and a score of 3 to 7 can happen by luck. Draw a bar chart with one bar for each distance.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you act like a fish. You keep your hands still in water and try to tell which side a ripple came from, without seeing or hearing it.

setup.art: A wide steel basin on a towel with 4 centimetres of water, and a child with a scarf over her eyes and both hands flat in the middle of the water.
setup.caption: 1. Rest both hands flat in the middle of the basin. Cover your eyes and ears.

setup.art: A helper holding a card strip over the water with one end above the child's left hand, and a fingertip about to dip at the other end.
setup.caption: 2. Measure the distance with the strip. Dip one fingertip once.

setup.art: A helper tossing a coin beside the basin, with the words heads is left and tails is right written on a card.
setup.caption: 3. A coin toss decides left or right.

setup.art: A results table with three rows for 5, 10 and 20 centimetres, and tick marks for right answers.
setup.caption: 4. Score each try. Do 10 tries at each distance.

flow.do: Show your child the basin. Ask for their guesses and reasons. Write them at the top of the results table.
flow.say: Fish have a line of tiny sensors along their sides that feel water move. Can your hands do anything like it? Will you tell which side a ripple came from? Will you at 20 centimetres? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Fish feel water move. Can your hands? Guess first. Will you tell left from right? Why?

ask.q: What do you think your hands will feel when a ripple reaches them?
good: A tiny wobble.
Nothing at all when it is far.
A touch like a very light tickle.

flow.parent: Do not tell what a lateral line is yet. Let your child make their guess first. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Ripple Skin test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Put the towel on a low, flat table or the floor. Put the basin on it with 4 centimetres of water. Your child kneels or sits beside it. The long side of the basin faces them. They put both hands flat in the middle of the water, with fingers spread. They close their eyes and the scarf or cap goes over their eyes and ears. Cut a card strip 20 centimetres long. Mark it at 5 and 10 centimetres.
flow.say: Put both hands flat in the middle of the water. Keep them still, like a fish resting. Close your eyes, and we cover your ears, so you cannot hear or see anything. Only your skin will tell you.
flow.kid: Put both hands in the water. Keep them still. Close your eyes.
flow.parent: Wait until the water is completely still before every ripple. This takes 5 to 10 seconds. If the child's hands touch the sides, move the basin so that the hands sit in the middle. Distances are measured from the nearer hand, along the long side of the basin, so the dip stays well inside the basin wall. If your basin is shorter than 60 centimetres, test 5, 10 and 15 centimetres instead, and write the new distance in the table. Roles: one child (or the parent) keeps the hands still, one tosses the coin and dips the finger, and one scores. With 2 to 4 children, each child does their own 10 tries at every distance and then swaps. Dip with the same finger, the same depth and the same quickness every time, and stay still and quiet afterwards, because the dipper's breathing or a bumped table can give the answer away.

check.q: Why do we cover the child's ears and eyes?
options: So only the skin of the hands can sense the ripple
So the child does not get scared
So the water stays still
check.why: A dip makes a tiny sound and a flicker of movement. If the child could hear or see it, that would tell them the side. We want to know only what the skin alone can sense.

flow.context: In this step, you set up the basin and cover your child's eyes and ears.

flow.do: Start with 5 centimetres. Toss the coin. Heads means the left side, and tails means the right side. Hold the strip above the water with one end over the child's hand on that side. Dip one fingertip, 1 centimetre deep, at the other end. Quickly lift it out and keep still. Ask 'left or right?' Do 10 tries. Count the right answers.
flow.say: I will make one small ripple, then you say left or right. Wait until I say go. I make the ripple 5 centimetres from your hand.
flow.kid: Feel for the ripple. Say left or right. Try ten times.
flow.parent: Wait for still water between tries. Do not say if the answer is right until the end of the 10. Your child may get nearly all 10 right here. This is the closest distance.
flow.context: In this step, you test ripples that start 5 centimetres from the hand.

flow.do: Now test 10 centimetres in the same way. Use the strip to measure from the child's hand. Toss the coin each time, and wait for still water. Do 10 tries and count the right answers.
flow.say: Now the ripple will start further away, 10 centimetres from your hand. Feel for it, and say left or right.
flow.kid: Now the ripple is farther away. Say left or right.

ask.q: Was it easier or harder than before? What did your hands feel?
good: Harder, the ripple was weaker.
I guessed more.
I felt a tiny wobble sometimes.

flow.parent: Expect the score to drop for most children, but it varies. Keep the same gentle dip, not a bigger one.
flow.context: In this step, you test ripples that start 10 centimetres from the hand.

flow.do: Last, test 20 centimetres. Use the strip again. Toss the coin each time and wait for still water. Do 10 tries and count the right answers.
flow.say: The last ripple will be further still, 20 centimetres from your hand. Feel for it, and say left or right. It is fine to guess.
flow.kid: The ripple is far now. Say left or right. Guess if you must.

check.q: At 20 centimetres, your child gets 5 right out of 10. What does that mean?
options: About what pure guessing gives, so the skin felt little at that distance
Their hands are broken
The test is no good
check.why: If a child guessed every time, they would get about 5 out of 10 by luck. A score close to 5 means the ripple was too weak for the skin to sense. It does not mean anything is wrong. It is a real result.

flow.parent: If your child still gets 9 or 10, try 30 centimetres in a bigger tub. If you get about 5 out of 10 even at 5 centimetres, check that the hands are really still and dip a little deeper, the same each time, and try again. Water this shallow gives only a faint ripple, so low scores at 20 centimetres are normal. If the score is near 5, that is real data. Say so.
flow.context: In this step, you test ripples that start 20 centimetres from the hand.

flow.do: Write the three scores in the table. Draw a bar chart. Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why. Then tell them how a lateral line works.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened? Now I will tell you what a fish has that you do not.
flow.kid: Draw a bar for each distance. Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.
flow.think: A fish has sensors along her whole side. What could she find that you could not?
flow.parent: After your child's own words, say: a fish has a line of tiny sensors along each side with hairs that bend when water moves. She feels where another fish is, even in muddy or dark water. Your hands have no such sensors, but skin can still feel big ripples. A fish feels water movement only a short way, about one or two body lengths, so distance matters for her too.
flow.context: In this step, you draw your results and meet the lateral line.

experiments.title: Cup Your Ears: do ear flaps help you hear?
experiments.question: A fox turns her large ear flaps towards a sound. Do hands cupped behind your ears help you hear a quiet sound from farther away, and does it matter which way they face?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Will cupped hands help you hear a ticking clock from farther away? What if the hands face backwards? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The same ticking clock is held at the same height, pointing at your child, every time. The room, the helper and the way the helper walks stay the same. Your child keeps their eyes closed and does not move their head. Only the position of the ears changes. Each condition is tested twice, because one try can be a fluke.

materials.item: a clock with a quiet tick, or a phone playing a very soft steady beep (a wristwatch is only heard within about 50 centimetres, so start 1 metre away with it)
a quiet room or corridor at least 3 metres long, with fans and TV switched off
a tape measure or a ruler and a long string, a stool or chair for sitting, and a strip of tape or chalk marks every 20 centimetres on the floor
a sheet of thick card, rolled into a cone about 20 centimetres long, and tape
a scarf for closing the eyes (or the child can just shut their eyes)
the results table and a pencil

experiments.safety: Keep the clock volume soft. Never use a loud sound near ears. The helper walks slowly and quietly, and the walkway is clear of stools and bags, to avoid tripping. A child with a cold or ear pain should not do this test. Never poke anything into an ear: the cone is held against the ear and never pushed in.
experiments.record: For each setting, write the distance in centimetres where your child first heard the tick, the best of two tries. Draw a bar chart with one bar for each setting.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you find out whether hands cupped behind your ears, in the way a fox's ear flaps work, help you to hear a quiet sound from farther away.

setup.art: A child sitting on a stool with eyes closed in a corridor, and a helper far away holding a small ticking clock at the child's ear height.
setup.caption: 1. Sit still with your eyes closed. The helper starts far away with the clock.

setup.art: The helper walking slowly towards the child, with a tape measure laid along the floor.
setup.caption: 2. The helper comes closer, slowly. Say now when you first hear the tick.

setup.art: The child with both hands cupped behind the ears, fingers pointing forwards, and a second picture with the hands cupped backwards.
setup.caption: 3. Test with cupped hands pointing forwards, and then backwards.

setup.art: A rolled card cone held at the child's ear with the wide end facing the clock.
setup.caption: 4. Last, test a card cone at one ear.

flow.do: Show your child the clock, your cupped hands and the cone. Ask for their guesses and reasons. Write them at the top of the results table.
flow.say: Foxes, cats and deer have big ear flaps that they turn towards a sound. Do you think cupped hands could do the same job? What if the hands face backwards? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Foxes turn big ears towards sounds. Can your hands do that? Guess first. Why?

ask.q: What do you think an ear flap does?
good: It catches sound.
It points sound into the ear.
It makes the ear bigger.

flow.parent: Do not explain what an ear flap does yet. Let your child guess first.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Cup Your Ears test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Pick a quiet room or corridor. Put the stool at one end. Lay the tape measure along the floor in front of the stool. Your child sits on the stool, facing along the tape, with eyes closed. Check that the clock ticks softly and steadily. Show your child what the tick sounds like before they close their eyes.
flow.say: Sit here and close your eyes. I will walk towards you with the clock. Say now when you first hear it tick. Keep your head still.
flow.kid: Sit and close your eyes. Say now when you hear the tick.
flow.parent: Switch off fans and noisy things. A tick is easy to guess at, so tell the helper to walk to the same speed every time and not to pause when the child is about to answer. If you cannot find a clock, a phone playing a soft steady beep works. Turn the beep volume down until it is only just audible at 1 metre. Typical hearing distances for a quiet tick are from half a metre to a few metres, so your numbers may be different. If the child hears it at the 3 metre start, the clock is too loud. If they never hear it, start closer. Roles: the listener sits with eyes closed, one helper walks with the clock, and one reads the distance and writes it down. One child with a parent: the parent walks, then reads the tape. With 2 to 4 children, take turns as listener, and the others wait silently, because anyone who hears the tick can give it away. Each child makes a row in the table.
flow.context: In this step, you set up the quiet room and the clock.

flow.do: Test bare ears first. The helper starts 3 metres away, holding the clock at ear height, pointing at the child. The helper walks towards the child, about 20 centimetres every 3 seconds, one mark at a time. The child says 'now' when they hear the tick. Measure the distance from the clock to the child's ear. Do it twice.
flow.say: Listen carefully, and say now the first moment you hear the tick. Do not guess before you hear it.
flow.kid: Listen. Say now when you hear the tick.

ask.q: How far away was the clock when you first heard it?
good: About one metre.
Quite close.
Not very far.

flow.parent: The helper walks slowly and quietly, with no talking. Drop the clock to the child's ear height. If the child hears it right at 3 metres, the clock is too loud. Turn it down.
flow.context: In this step, you find how far away your child hears the clock with bare ears.

flow.do: Now your child cups both hands behind their ears, with the fingers pointing forwards, towards the clock. The helper starts 3 metres away and walks closer as before, 20 centimetres every 3 seconds. Measure the distance when the child says 'now'. Do it twice. Then do one more bare-ear try. This checks that practice alone did not help.
flow.say: Cup your hands behind your ears, like a fox. Keep your eyes closed. Say now when you first hear the tick.
flow.kid: Cup your hands behind your ears. Say now when you hear the tick.

check.q: Your child hears the tick from 120 centimetres with bare ears, and from 160 centimetres with cupped hands. What does this suggest?
options: The cupped hands caught more sound
The clock got louder
The child's ears got bigger
check.why: The cupped hands work as a bigger ear flap. They catch more of the sound and guide it into the ear, so a weaker tick can still be heard. The clock and the child's ears did not change.

flow.context: In this step, you test cupped hands pointing forwards.

flow.do: Now your child cups both hands behind their ears with the fingers pointing backwards, away from the clock. The helper starts 3 metres away and walks closer as before, 20 centimetres every 3 seconds. Measure the distance when the child says 'now'. Do it twice.
flow.say: Now turn your cupped hands to face behind you, like a fox looking the other way. Say now when you first hear the tick.
flow.kid: Turn your hands to face backwards. Say now when you hear the tick.

ask.q: Was it easier or harder this time? Why do you think so?
good: Harder, the hands blocked the sound.
The sound had to go round.
The hands pointed the wrong way.

flow.parent: Most people hear the tick from a shorter distance with hands facing backwards than with bare ears. The hands now catch sound from behind, and the sound from the front has to go round them.
flow.context: In this step, you test cupped hands pointing the wrong way.

flow.do: Last, hold the card cone to one ear, with the wide end facing the clock. Do the walking test once more. Measure the distance when the child says 'now'.
flow.say: This cone is a bigger ear. Hold the small end to your ear, with the wide end pointing at me. Say now when you hear the tick.
flow.kid: Hold the cone to your ear. Say now when you hear the tick.
flow.parent: The cone often does best of all. Make sure the child holds the small end gently to the ear and does not push it in. The cone is on one ear only, so keep the other ear open, and compare it with a bare ear. If cupped hands or the cone make no difference, the room may be noisy or the clock too loud. Write the honest result and ask why.
flow.context: In this step, you test a paper cone as a bigger ear.

flow.do: Write the best distance for each setting. Draw a bar chart. Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened? Which animal would use cupped ears like these?
flow.kid: Draw a bar for each setting. Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.
flow.think: A fox hunts mice that squeak under the grass. How does her ear shape help?
flow.parent: After your child's words, say: an ear flap collects more sound and points it into the ear, and it can be turned to find where the sound comes from. Ear flaps are an animal's way of being a bigger ear. Mammals have them. Birds, frogs and snakes do not.
flow.context: In this step, you draw your results and think about animals' ears.

activities.title: One Pond, Five Worlds: sort what each group senses best

materials.item: plain paper, scissors and a pencil
a big sheet of paper or the back of a calendar, for the table
coloured pencils

schedule.what: Cut out the clue strips. Sort them under the five groups. Then draw the pond as one of the animals might sense it.

activities.record: A sheet with five columns, one for each group, the clue strips stuck under the right ones, and a count under each column. Then a drawing of the pond as one group senses it.
activities.context: In this activity, you sort clues about animal senses into the five groups of animals with a backbone, and then you draw the same pond as one of them might sense it.

setup.art: A table with fifteen small paper strips in a pile, each with a short sentence about a sense.
setup.caption: 1. Write the fifteen clues on strips of paper.

setup.art: A big sheet of paper with five columns labelled fish, amphibian, reptile, bird and mammal, with some strips already stuck in.
setup.caption: 2. Sort the strips under the five groups.

setup.art: A child's drawing of a pond as a snake might sense it, with warm shapes glowing orange and cool shapes dark blue.
setup.caption: 3. Draw the pond as one group might sense it.

flow.do: Write each clue on its own strip. Strip 1, a line of tiny sensors along the sides feels ripples. Strip 2, heat pits on the lips sense a warm body. Strip 3, a round eardrum sits on the outside of the head. Strip 4, a fourth colour cone sees ultraviolet. Strip 5, three tiny middle-ear bones. Strip 6, a forked tongue gathers scent. Strip 7, whiskers feel moving water and air. Strip 8, ear flaps turn towards a sound. Strip 9, a heart-shaped face collects sound. Strip 10, eyes on the sides give a very wide view. Strip 11, tiny dark dots on the jaws feel ripples. Strip 12, sharks sense weak electricity. Strip 13, a tadpole has a lateral line. Strip 14, high clicks and echoes find prey. Strip 15, the nose has many more smell receptors than a person's.
flow.say: Each strip is a clue about a sense. Some belong to one group only. Some could belong to more than one. Read them aloud, and think about who has this sense.
flow.kid: Write each clue on a strip. Read them all.
flow.parent: The clues cover all five groups. Strips 3, 10 and 13 are good for discussion. An eardrum on the outside is true for frogs. Wide eyes are true for fish, frogs, birds and many mammals. A tadpole is an amphibian. There are no wrong answers to the discussion. Cutting strips: a child of 6 to 7 should use blunt, child-safe scissors with an adult close. With 2 to 4 children, each writes and cuts about five strips, then everybody sorts together. One child with a parent: share the writing.
flow.context: In this step, you write the fifteen clues on paper strips.

flow.do: Draw five columns on the big sheet. Write one group at the top of each. Read a strip and decide where it belongs. Stick it there. If a strip could fit two groups, put it between them and say why. When all 15 are placed, count the strips under each group. Write the counts under the columns. Which group has most strips? Is that because it has the most senses, or because we know most about it?
flow.say: Put each strip where it belongs. If two groups could fit, put it in the middle. Then tell me why.
flow.kid: Put each strip in the right column. Explain your choice.

ask.q: Which strip was the hardest to place? Why?
good: Wide eyes, because many groups have them.
The tadpole, because they change shape.
The strips that fit two groups.

check.q: A strip says: eardrum on the outside of the head, with no ear flap. Which group fits best?
options: Amphibians, such as a frog
Mammals, such as a dog
Fish, such as a rohu
check.why: A frog has a round eardrum on the skin of her head. Dogs have ear flaps. Fish have no eardrum on the outside at all, because sound passes through their bodies to the inner ear. Birds and many reptiles also have eardrums, so the strip fits more than one group. But a frog is the clearest example.

flow.parent: Many answers are partly right. Some strips fit two or three groups, such as wide eyes and eardrums. Ask your child to give their reason. Reasons matter more than the exact column. Counts depend on where you put the shared strips, so write what you got. Do not look for one right answer.
flow.context: In this step, you sort the clue strips under the five groups.

flow.do: Choose one group. Draw a pond as that group might sense it. Use colours or shapes for what it senses. Add a label that says what you think is most important to that animal.
flow.say: Draw the pond as a fish, a python or a pigeon might sense it. What would stand out? What would hardly be there at all? Use colour or shape to show it.
flow.kid: Draw the pond as another animal senses it. What stands out?

ask.q: What stands out most to your animal? What would hardly matter?
good: Moving things stand out to a frog.
Warm things glow for a python.
Smells stand out for a dog.

flow.parent: There is no correct picture. A snake may show warm shapes bright and cool shapes dark. A fish may show ripples as lines. A dog may show smell trails. Praise the thinking, and ask what each choice shows.
flow.context: In this step, you draw the pond as another animal might sense it.

flow.do: Ask your child to show the drawing to the family. Ask the family to guess which animal it is.
flow.say: Let us show this to the family. Can they guess which animal is sensing the pond? What clue helped?
flow.kid: Show your drawing. Can they guess your animal?
flow.think: If you could be this animal for a day, what would you miss most about being you?
flow.context: In this step, you share the drawing and see if others can guess the animal.

activities.title: Warm Spot Finder: which part of your skin feels warmth from the farthest?

materials.item: 2 identical steel or thick plastic pots or tall tumblers, about 12 to 15 centimetres tall (a bigger warm side is felt from farther than a small mug)
comfortably hot water, as hot as a bath you can sit in, about 45 to 50 degrees in typical terms, mixed from the tap or kettle with cool water and tested by an adult on the inside of the wrist
water at room temperature, in the second pot
a ruler
a scarf for closing the eyes, a pencil and paper

schedule.what: Prepare the pots. Test four parts of the skin. Compare the distances.

activities.record: A table with four rows, palm, back of the hand, fingertip and cheek, and for each the distance in centimetres where your child first felt warmth. Write 'touched' if nothing was felt before 2 centimetres.
activities.context: In this activity, you act a little like a snake with heat pits. You find which part of your skin feels the warmth of a pot from the farthest away.

setup.art: Two identical pots on a table, one marked with a small dot on the bottom, with a ruler beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Fill one pot with hot-bath-warm water and one with room-temperature water.

setup.art: A child with a scarf over the eyes holding out a palm while a helper brings a pot slowly closer from the side.
setup.caption: 2. Bring a pot slowly towards the skin. The child says warm or not warm.

setup.art: A table with four rows, palm, back of hand, fingertip and cheek, with distances written in.
setup.caption: 3. Test four places on the skin and write the distances.

flow.do: An adult fills one pot with hot-bath-warm water. Check that it feels comfortably warm on the inside of your wrist, and never hot. A finger should stay in it for 10 seconds without pain, and the outside of the pot should be bearable to hold. Fill the other pot with room-temperature water. Put a small secret mark under the warm pot. Ask your child to guess which part of the skin will feel warmth from farthest, and why.
flow.say: Today you will find warmth with your skin, the way a python does with her lip pits. Which part of your skin will notice it first? The palm, the back of your hand, a fingertip or your cheek? Why?
flow.kid: Guess first. Which part of your skin feels warmth best? Why?

ask.q: Why might one part of the skin be better at it than another?
good: It has thinner skin.
It has more tiny sensors.
It is used to touching things.

flow.parent: The warm water must be comfortable to touch, never hot. The adult prepares and checks the water. The pots must look identical so your child cannot guess by sight. Warm water cools fast, so refill the warm pot after about 10 minutes, and check again with your wrist. Warmth is usually felt only within a few centimetres.
