Warmth from a pot is felt only close up: often from 3 to 15 centimetres, and sometimes only a few centimetres, so the numbers are small. This is real data. The adult always holds the pot and stops 2 centimetres from the skin, and nobody touches it. Do not use hotter water, and keep it out of the way of small hands. Roles: with a parent, the parent holds and writes. With 2 to 4 children, one is tested at a time with eyes closed, one holds the pot, one writes, and the others stay silent. Each child can test the palm and cheek and compare, since skin differs between people.
flow.context: In this step, you prepare two pots, one warm and one at room temperature, and make a guess.

flow.do: Your child closes their eyes. Hold one pot, picked at random, 30 centimetres from their palm, to the side. Move it 2 centimetres closer every 3 seconds, and stop at 2 centimetres from the skin. The child says 'warm' or 'not warm' each time. Write the distance where they first say 'warm' for the warm pot. Then swap in the other pot, to check that 'not warm' is said for it.
flow.say: Close your eyes and hold out your palm. I bring a pot closer slowly. Say warm if you feel warmth, and not warm if you do not. Tell me the moment you feel it.
flow.kid: Close your eyes. Say warm or not warm.
flow.parent: Use the cool pot a few times as a check, so your child cannot just say warm every time. Hold the pot at the same height each time, and bring it from the side so rising warm air does not give it away.

check.q: Why do we sometimes bring the room-temperature pot?
options: To check that the child is not just saying warm every time
To make the test longer
To keep the first pot cold
check.why: If the child said warm for both pots, the answers would mean nothing. Using the cool pot as a control shows that the child can tell the difference.

flow.context: In this step, you test the palm for warmth from a distance.

flow.do: Repeat with the back of the hand, a fingertip, and the cheek. Always start 30 centimetres away, come in 2 centimetres every 3 seconds, and stop at 2 centimetres. Write the distance where your child first says 'warm'.
flow.say: Now the back of your hand. Then your fingertip. Then your cheek. Same game. Say warm the moment you feel it.
flow.kid: Now test the back of the hand, a fingertip, and your cheek.

ask.q: Which place noticed the warmth from farthest? Which was the last?
good: The cheek, it is thin.
The palm.
The fingertip was the last.

flow.parent: Many people notice warmth on the cheek or the palm first, and the back of the hand or fingertip later. Your child's order may differ. Write down what you get. Differences of one or two centimetres between places are within the error of the test, so look for big gaps only. Repeat the cheek and the back of the hand if the answers are close.
flow.context: In this step, you test three more places on the skin.

flow.do: Draw a bar chart of the four distances. Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why. Then explain pit organs.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think? What did you see? Why did it happen? A python has pits on her lips that notice warmth. Some pit snakes sense a very small difference in warmth.
flow.kid: Draw a bar for each place. Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.
flow.think: Your skin feels warmth, but a python feels it much more finely. What would she be able to do?
flow.parent: After your child's words, say: some snakes have heat pits that react to infrared. An Indian rock python has rows of pits along her lips, and she can find a warm rat in the dark. Measurements on pit vipers have found that they have been reported to respond to changes of about three thousandths of a degree. Cobras do not have pits.
flow.context: In this step, you draw your results and meet the heat pit.

flow.do: Dry the pots and pour the water down the sink. Wash your hands.
flow.say: Well done. Tell me one thing you would like to try with the pots next time.
flow.kid: Clean up. What would you try next time?
flow.context: In this step, you clean up and think of another test.

activities.title: Nose Trail: follow a smell on the floor with two nostrils, and with one

materials.item: a piece of string or a strip of cloth, about 3 metres long
a strong but safe smell, such as vanilla essence, or crushed cardamom or ground coffee
a scarf for closing the eyes
an old towel or cloth to kneel on
paper and a pencil for scoring

schedule.what: Lay the scent trail. Follow it with both nostrils, and then with one nostril closed. Compare how well it went.

activities.record: A table with two rows, both nostrils open and one nostril closed. For each, write how far your child followed the trail before they lost it, in steps.
activities.context: In this activity, you follow a smell trail on the floor like a dog or a snake, with your eyes closed. You find out if two nostrils help.

setup.art: A long string laid in a gentle zigzag across a clean floor, with small dabs of vanilla marked along it.
setup.caption: 1. Lay a 3 metre string in a zigzag, and dab it with scent every 20 centimetres.

setup.art: A child on hands and knees with a scarf over her eyes, sniffing along the floor near the string.
setup.caption: 2. Follow the smell with your nose, eyes closed.

setup.art: The same child gently pinching one nostril closed and trying again.
setup.caption: 3. Close one nostril and try again on a new trail.

flow.do: Lay the string in a gentle zigzag on a clean floor. Dab a little scent on the string every 20 centimetres. Use only a few drops each time. Ask your child to guess whether two nostrils or one will follow the trail better, and why.
flow.say: Dogs follow smell trails with their noses to the ground. A snake flicks her forked tongue to catch scent from two sides. Do you think two nostrils help you follow a trail better than one? Why?
flow.kid: Guess first. Do two nostrils follow a trail better than one? Why?
flow.parent: First ask whether anyone is allergic or sensitive to the scent, and choose another if so. Use scents that are safe to sniff. Do not use strong sprays, cleaning liquids or anything that irritates the nose. Keep the room well aired, and put the used string out of the room between trails, because the smell lingers. Sniffing one strong smell for a while tires the nose, so rest for a few minutes between trails. A cloth strip works better than thin string because it holds more scent. Roles: one child follows the trail, one lays it, one counts the steps, and one walks beside to keep the follower safe. One child with a parent: the parent lays the trail and walks beside. With 2 to 4 children, each child follows both a two-nostril and a one-nostril trail, and some begin with the one-nostril trail so the order does not decide the result. Keep the follower's path clear of furniture and corners, and the others stay out of sight of the trail.
flow.context: In this step, you lay a scent trail and make a guess.

flow.do: Cover your child's eyes with the scarf. They kneel at the start of the trail and sniff along it, keeping their nose near the floor. They follow with the nose only, and do not feel for the string with their hands. Walk beside them to keep them safe. Count how many steps they follow before they lose the trail. Write the count.
flow.say: Keep your eyes closed, and sniff along the floor. Follow the smell as far as you can. Tell me when you lose it.
flow.kid: Close your eyes. Sniff along the floor. Follow the smell.
flow.parent: The helper stays close to stop bumps. Do not guide with words. If the child loses the trail, say 'You lost it' and note where.

check.q: Why does the child keep their nose near the floor?
options: The smell is strongest where the scent is, near the floor
To keep the scarf on
To see better
check.why: Scent sits on the string and the floor. The air higher up holds much less of it. A dog also keeps her nose near the ground when she follows a trail.

flow.context: In this step, your child follows the trail with both nostrils open.

flow.do: Lay a new trail of the same length, in a different zigzag. Dab the same amount of scent. Now your child pinches one nostril closed gently and follows it. Count the steps before they lose it. Write the count.
flow.say: Pinch one nostril closed. Now follow a new trail. Keep your nose near the floor.
flow.kid: Pinch one nostril. Follow the new trail.

ask.q: Did closing one nostril change how you followed the trail? How?
good: I lost it sooner.
I wasn't sure which way to turn.
It was about the same.

flow.parent: In a 2007 study at the University of California, Berkeley, people did better at following a scent trail with both nostrils open. A snake's two-pronged tongue may work in a similar way, by sampling scent from two sides. Your child's results may differ, so write what you see. If time allows, follow a third trail with both nostrils to check that a tired nose or practice was not the cause. Honest results can go either way, because one try is only one try.
flow.context: In this step, your child follows a new trail with one nostril closed.

flow.do: Write both counts in the table. Draw a bar chart. Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why. Then explain what a forked tongue does.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think? What did you see? Why do you think it happened? A snake flicks her forked tongue to taste the air on two sides. What could two sides tell her?
flow.kid: Draw two bars. Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.
flow.think: Why would a snake with a forked tongue find a trail more easily than one with a single tip?
flow.parent: A strong answer may say that two samples let the animal compare left and right, and turn towards the stronger one. After your child's words, say: a snake's forked tongue collects scent and wipes it onto two spots in the roof of her mouth. The two tips may help her work out which way the trail goes.
flow.context: In this step, you compare your two counts and think about the snake's tongue.

flow.do: Wash the string, or throw it away. Wipe the floor if the scent has marked it. Wash your hands.
flow.say: Clean up. Which smells were easy to follow, and which were hard?
flow.kid: Clean up. Wash your hands.
flow.context: In this step, you clean up and think about which smells were easy to follow.

games.title: Whose World? guess the group from the sense
games.context: This is a guessing game. Each card describes a sense. You guess which group of animals with a backbone it belongs to, and the back of the card tells you.
rules: Cut out the 24 two-sided cards and the 5 group tokens. Make a set of 5 tokens for each player.
Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile with the clue side up. One player is the reader.
The reader reads the front of the top card aloud and keeps the back hidden.
Every other player secretly puts one group token face down: fish, amphibian, reptile, bird or mammal.
Everyone turns their token over together.
The reader reads the back. The back begins with the group or groups it fits. A player scores 1 point if their token is one of those groups.
The reader reads the explanation on the back. Anyone who disagrees can say why.
The reader's job passes to the player on the left after every card. With two players, take turns being the reader.
When the pile is finished, the player with the most points wins. A tie is a shared win.

setup.art: A table with a pile of clue cards face up and five group tokens in a row in front of each player.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and tokens. Put the cards in a pile.

setup.art: One player reading a card aloud, with the others each putting a token face down.
setup.caption: 2. The reader reads the clue. Everyone picks a token.

setup.art: The tokens turned over together and the reader showing the back of the card.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the tokens over. The reader shows the back.

printables.title: 24 two-sided cards: a sense clue on the front, and the group and reason on the back

items.f: I feel a ripple along my side from an insect that fell in the water. I cannot see it.
items.b: Fish. The lateral line is a row of tiny sensors along the side that feel moving water.

items.f: I have a round eardrum on the outside of my head and no ear flap. I call loudly in the first monsoon rains.
items.b: Amphibian. A frog's eardrum sits flat on the skin behind the eye.

items.f: I have tiny pits along my lips that sense the heat of a warm body.
items.b: Reptile. An Indian rock python finds a warm rat with her lip pits.

items.f: I can see ultraviolet light, which people cannot see.
items.b: Bird, Fish or Reptile. Most birds have a fourth kind of colour cone that senses ultraviolet. Many fish, turtles and some lizards do too.

items.f: I have three tiny bones in my middle ear.
items.b: Mammal. Only mammals have three middle-ear bones.

items.f: I flick my forked tongue to gather scent from the air and the ground.
items.b: Reptile. A snake wipes the scent onto two spots in the roof of her mouth.

items.f: My whiskers can follow the swirl that a fish left in the water about half a minute ago.
items.b: Mammal. A harbour seal does this with her whiskers.

items.f: I can find a fish hiding under sand by the weak electricity of its muscles.
items.b: Fish. Sharks and rays have electric sense.

items.f: My face is flat and shaped like a heart. It works like a dish to gather sound, and I catch a rat in the dark by hearing it.
items.b: Bird. A barn owl can find prey by sound alone.

items.f: My eyes sit on the sides of my head, and I can see almost all the way round.
items.b: Fish, Amphibian, Reptile, Bird or Mammal. Many animals that are hunted have side eyes. A pigeon sees about 340 degrees, and a horse also sees almost all the way round. Any token scores.

items.f: I call to other members of my family with sounds too low for people to hear.
items.b: Mammal. Asian elephants use infrasound.

items.f: I live in muddy river water and find fish by sending out high clicks and listening for the echoes.
items.b: Mammal. The Ganges river dolphin, called susu, has almost no use for her eyes.

items.f: I taste the mud with whiskers on my chin.
items.b: Fish. A magur catfish has taste cells on her whiskers.

items.f: My eyes bulge on top of my head so I can see above the water while my body hides.
items.b: Amphibian or Reptile. A frog and a mugger crocodile both do this.

items.f: I have tiny dark dots on my jaws that feel ripples and pressure.
items.b: Reptile. A mugger crocodile can feel a fish swim near her without seeing the fish.

items.f: My nose has many tens of times more smell receptors than a person's nose.
items.b: Mammal. A dog has many more smell receptors than a person has.

items.f: I can see colours in light so dim that a person sees only grey.
items.b: Reptile. Some geckos do, according to experiments.

items.f: I feel the ground shake through my jaw bone, because I have no outer ear.
items.b: Reptile. A snake picks up vibrations from the ground.

items.f: I turn my ear flaps one at a time to find where a sound is coming from.
items.b: Mammal. A cat or a deer does this.

items.f: I send out calls too high for people to hear and listen for the echoes to find moths in the dark.
items.b: Mammal. A small bat, such as the Indian pipistrelle, uses echolocation.

items.f: When I was young I had a lateral line like a fish. I lost it when I left the water.
items.b: Amphibian. A tadpole feels ripples with a lateral line, like a fish.

items.f: I smell carrion from far away, though most of my group smells little.
items.b: Bird. A turkey vulture can find food by smell.

items.f: I seem to use the Earth's magnetic field to find my way on a long journey, and scientists still argue about how.
items.b: Fish, Reptile or Bird. Some fish, sea turtles and many birds seem to. The receptor has not been found with certainty.

items.f: My eyes are at the front and my view is narrow, but I judge distance very well.
items.b: Bird or Mammal. An owl or a cat has eyes that overlap, which helps to judge how far away prey is.

printables.title: 5 group tokens for each player, cut from paper, one for each group

flow.do: Cut out the 24 cards and the 5 group tokens. Make one set of 5 tokens for each player. Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile with the clue side up.
flow.say: Each card has a clue about one sense. You guess which group of animals with a backbone it fits. The groups are fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards.
flow.context: This is the first step of Whose World? You set up the cards and the tokens.
flow.parent: The cards take a little while to cut, so one child cuts the cards while another cuts the tokens. Use blunt scissors for small children, with an adult close. With one child and a parent, there are two players: one reader and one guesser, and they swap after every card.

flow.do: Play the first six cards. The reader reads the front. Everyone picks a token and turns it over together. The reader reads the back. After card three, ask the question below.
flow.say: The reader reads the clue. Everyone picks a token. Turn them over together. Now read the back. Who scored? Who can say why?
flow.kid: The reader reads the clue. Pick a token. Turn it over. Check the back.

ask.q: Which clue was easy, and which was hard? Why?
good: The ones with only one group were easy.
The ones with many groups were hard.
I knew from the sense.

flow.parent: Some cards fit more than one group. The back begins with all the groups that fit. Anyone whose token matches any of them scores a point.
flow.context: In this step, you play the first six cards and learn how scoring works.

flow.do: Play the next nine cards. Pass the reader's job to the left after each card. After card twelve, ask the question below.
flow.say: Keep going. Pass the reader's job after every card. Remember to say why you chose your token.
flow.kid: Keep playing. Pass the reader's job after each card.

ask.q: Which sense did you not know an animal could have?
good: Electric sense in sharks.
Heat pits in a python.
Infrasound in elephants.

check.q: A card says: eyes on the sides of the head, nearly all the way round. Why does the back say any group can score?
options: Because animals in every group can have eyes like that
Because the card is a mistake
Because only fish have side eyes
check.why: Side eyes are common among animals that are hunted, in all five groups. The clue does not point to one group. A player who picks any group is right. Games sometimes have cards that teach by being open.

flow.context: In this step, you play the middle of the game and think about hard clues.

flow.do: Play the last nine cards. Count the points. The player with the most points wins. A tie is a shared win. Then ask the question below.
flow.say: Last cards. Then count the points. Who has the most? Which clue surprised you most?
flow.kid: Finish the cards. Count your points.
flow.think: If you could borrow one sense from these cards for a day, which would you choose?
flow.context: In this step, you finish the game, count points and share what surprised you.

games.title: Owl and Mice: catch a mouse by sound
games.players: 2 or more players, best in a big room or a corridor
games.context: This is an acting game. One player is the owl, who cannot see. The others are mice who try to cross the room without being heard. You find out how much an owl can do with ears alone.
rules: Mark a start line and a finish line on the floor, about 5 metres apart, with a chalk line or a strip of cloth.

One player is the owl. The owl sits on a low stool, or on a cushion on the floor, in the middle with eyes closed or a scarf over them, and holds a rolled newspaper for pointing. The owl only points and never hits.
The other players are mice. They stand behind the start line.
The owl cannot move from the stool. The owl can turn the whole head and body.

When the owl says 'go', the mice try to creep to the finish line without being heard, one slow step about every 2 seconds, the same for all. Everyone plays in socks or bare feet on a clear floor, with no chairs or bags in the way.
If the owl hears a mouse, she points the rolled paper at that mouse. If she points straight at the mouse, the mouse is caught and goes back to the start.

Round 1: the owl listens with bare ears. Round 2: the owl cups both hands behind the ears. Round 3: the mice walk on sheets of newspaper laid on the floor, held flat with a little tape so they do not slide. Wet tiles are slippery, so do not use wet or polished floors.

Each mouse crosses three times in every round, so there are enough tries to compare. With only two players, the mouse crosses six times in each round. Count the crossings that were not heard. Swap owls whenever you like, so everyone gets a turn. There is no winner. Talk about what changed. Small counts can change by luck, so only a big change means something.

setup.art: A long room with a start line, a finish line, a stool in the middle with a blindfolded child holding a rolled newspaper, and three children at the start line.
setup.caption: 1. Mark the lines. The owl sits blindfolded on the stool in the middle.

setup.art: Three children creeping on tiptoe across the room towards the finish line, while the blindfolded owl turns her head towards a sound.
setup.caption: 2. The mice creep. The owl listens and points.

setup.art: The owl with both hands cupped behind her ears and newspapers laid on the floor.
setup.caption: 3. Try again with cupped hands, and then with newspaper on the floor.

printables.title: A score sheet with one line for each round, and a place to write how many crossings were not heard
items: Round 1, bare ears: crossings that were not heard
Round 2, cupped hands: crossings that were not heard
Round 3, newspaper on the floor: crossings that were not heard

flow.do: Mark the start and finish lines. Choose the owl. Explain that the owl cannot see, and cannot leave the stool.
flow.say: A barn owl can catch a mouse in a dark room by sound alone. In this game, one of us is the owl. The owl cannot see, and cannot get up. The rest of us are mice. Can the mice cross?
flow.kid: One of you is the owl. The owl cannot see. The others are mice.
flow.context: This is the first step of Owl and Mice. You set up the room and choose the owl.

flow.do: Play Round 1. The owl uses bare ears. The mice creep from the start line to the finish line. The owl points at any mouse she hears. Count the crossings that were not heard.
flow.say: Mice, creep as quietly as you can. Owl, listen carefully. Point at any mouse you hear. Owl, say go.
flow.kid: Mice, creep quietly. Owl, listen and point.

ask.q: Owl, how did you know where a mouse was?
good: I turned towards the soft sound.
I heard where it came from.
I turned my head until the sound was in front.

flow.parent: The pointing must be straight at the mouse, within an arm's length of it. The owl's skill is in turning the head until the sound is in front of the face. Notice if this happens. With one child and a parent, the parent is the mouse and the child is the owl, and then swap. The owl must not peek, and mice should not talk or giggle. Play in a quiet place, with the fans and the TV off.
flow.context: In this step, you play the first round with bare ears.

flow.do: Play Round 2. The owl cups both hands behind the ears, fingers forward. Play as before. Count the crossings that were not heard. Then play Round 3 with newspaper laid on the floor for the mice to walk on.
flow.say: Owl, cup your hands behind your ears. Mice, creep again. Then we put down newspaper, and the mice walk on it. What changes?
flow.kid: Owl, cup your hands. Mice, creep again. Then walk on newspaper.

check.q: The mice walk on newspaper and are caught much more often. Why?
options: Newspaper rustles, so the sound is louder and easier to hear
The owl can see the paper
The mice get tired
check.why: Rustling makes a louder, sharper sound. In the story and in real life, barn owls drop onto a rustling sound even when nothing is there. Dry leaves are an owl's friend and a mouse's problem.

flow.context: In this step, you play the rounds with cupped hands and newspaper.

flow.do: Swap the owl. Play any round again. Then talk about what changed in each round.
flow.say: Swap the owl and play again. Which round was easiest for the owl? Which was hardest? What is a mouse's best way to stay safe from an owl?
flow.kid: Swap the owl. Play again. What changed?
flow.think: How could a mouse cross a dry-leaf floor without being heard? What would an owl need to change?
flow.parent: Talk about how real mice freeze when they hear an owl, and how rustling leaves make hunting easier for the owl. No winner is needed.
flow.context: In this step, you swap places and talk about what changed.

projects.title: Window Watch: how a pigeon or crow uses her eyes and ears

materials.item: a window, balcony, terrace or garden where pigeons, crows or sparrows visit
a notebook and pencil
a few grains of rice or bajra to sprinkle on a ledge, from a distance (a tape measure or counted steps for day 2)

projects.safety: Watch from a distance and do not try to touch or catch the bird. Wash hands after putting out grain. Do not lean out of a window or over a balcony rail. Put out only a small handful of grain, never bread or salty food, and sweep up what is left, so it does not attract rats or annoy neighbours. Avoid touching bird droppings.

schedule.what: Put out a few grains on a ledge, and sit quietly at a distance. Watch how a bird moves her head and which eye she turns towards you.
Watch again. Note how close you can get before she flies away, and what you were doing.
Watch for noises. Make a soft sound behind you and see if the bird turns her head. Write what you learnt.

projects.record: A notebook with three days of notes. For each day, write what the bird did with her head and eyes, how close you got before she flew away, and what she did when she heard a noise.
projects.context: In this project, you watch a bird in your own home or building over three days, and notice how she uses her sharp eyes and her ears.

setup.art: A child sitting quietly on a balcony floor with a notebook, watching a pigeon on a ledge a few metres away.
setup.caption: 1. Sit quietly and watch from a distance.

setup.art: A pigeon with her head tilted so that one eye faces the child, and an arrow showing the side view.
setup.caption: 2. Notice which eye she turns towards you.

setup.art: A notebook page with three days of drawings of bird head positions and notes.
setup.caption: 3. Draw and write what you notice each day.

flow.do: On day 1, put a few grains on a ledge, then sit quietly as far from the ledge as your space allows. On a terrace that is 3 to 4 metres. In a flat, sit behind the window glass. Watch the bird for 10 minutes. Note when she turns her head, which eye faces you, and whether her head bobs forward and back as she walks.
flow.say: Sit very still and watch the bird. Which eye is she using to look at you? Does her head bob as she walks? Draw what you see.
flow.kid: Sit still and watch a bird. Which eye looks at you? Draw her head.

ask.q: Why might a bird turn one side of her head towards you?
good: Her eyes are on the sides.
She sees you with one eye.
She wants a wide view.

flow.parent: Birds with side-facing eyes often turn one side towards something to look at it. A pigeon's head bob holds her view steady for a moment between steps. If no bird comes, repeat at another time of day, and early morning is usually best. Roles: with a parent, the parent keeps time and notes, and the child watches. With 2 to 4 children, one watches, one draws, one writes down, and everybody whispers. Share one window, and take turns at the front.
flow.context: In this step, you watch a bird and notice her eyes and her head movements.

flow.do: On day 2, sit in the same place. On a terrace or in a garden, move one slow step closer every 10 seconds. Count the steps. If you only have a window, move slowly behind the glass: lift a hand, then wave, then stand up. Note which move made her fly. Draw what you were doing when she left.
flow.say: Move one step closer every ten seconds. Stop when she flies. How close were you? Was she looking at you before she flew?
flow.kid: Move one slow step at a time. Stop when she flies. How close were you?
flow.parent: Measure the steps. From a window the bird may not fly at all, so write that down as a result. Do not chase. If the bird flies at once, start further away. Birds that watch you from the side may see you early.
flow.context: In this step, you find how close you can get before the bird flies away.

flow.do: On day 3, sit in the same place. While the bird feeds, make a soft sound behind you, such as a quiet tap on a steel plate. Tap once a minute, five times in all. After each tap, tally whether she looked up or turned her head, and which way. Also tally one minute with no tap. Write what you have found out over three days.
flow.say: Make a soft tap behind you. Does she turn her head? Which way? What do you think she is sensing? Write what you learnt.
flow.kid: Make a soft tap. Does she turn her head? Write what you learnt.
flow.think: What do you think a bird senses about you that you do not notice about yourself?
flow.context: In this step, you test if the bird turns towards a sound, and write what you learnt.
flow.parent: Compare the five tap minutes with a minute of no taps. If she looks up about as often with no tap, the tap did not matter. Real birds are unpredictable, so write the tally you really got.

challenges.title: Sound Catcher: build ears that hear a ticking clock from the farthest
challenges.problem: Build a pair of ears from card and tape that lets you hear a quiet ticking clock from the farthest distance.
constraints: Use only card, paper, tape and scissors.
The ears must be held or worn on the head, not held by a helper.
The clock stays at ear height and the same softness for every test.
Test your ears with your eyes closed, so that only the ears do the work.
materials: thick card or an old cereal box
a scarf for closing the eyes
general: A single cone held at one ear, with the wide end facing the sound.
Two cones, one for each ear, fixed to a headband.
A large dish shape behind the head, like a satellite dish, that catches sound and guides it forward.
creative: A fox-ear design: two tall pointed ears fixed to a headband, with the openings facing slightly forwards.
An owl-face dish: a big heart-shaped dish fixed around the face, with a gap for the ears.
Ears that turn: ear cones on hinges, so that you can aim one at a time, like a deer.
challenges.your_turn: Sketch your design first. Build it, and test it with your eyes closed. Find the farthest distance where you hear the tick. Then change one thing, such as the size of the opening, and test again. Which design worked best? Why do you think so?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about ear shapes. You build the best listening ears you can, and then test them.

setup.art: A child sketching three ear designs on paper: a single cone, two cones on a headband, and a big dish.
setup.caption: 1. Sketch some designs.

setup.art: A child building a card cone and taping it to a headband, with a tape measure and clock on the table.
setup.caption: 2. Build your ears from card and tape.

setup.art: A child wearing the ears with eyes closed, while a helper walks slowly towards her with a ticking clock.
setup.caption: 3. Test them. The helper walks closer until you hear the tick.

flow.do: Read the problem aloud. Ask your child to sketch two or three ear designs. Ask which animal's ears each one is like.
flow.say: Your job is to build ears that hear a quiet clock from farther than your own ears can. Sketch two or three designs first. Which animal is each design like?
flow.kid: Build ears that hear far. Sketch two or three designs first.

ask.q: What shape do you think catches the most sound?
good: A big cone.
A wide dish.
Something like a fox's ear.

flow.context: This is the start of the Sound Catcher challenge. You sketch your ideas first.

flow.do: First test bare ears, as in the Cup Your Ears experiment. Write the distance where your child first hears the tick. This is the number to beat.
flow.say: First, how far can you hear the clock with bare ears? That number is the one to beat.
flow.kid: Test bare ears first. This is the number to beat.
flow.context: In this step, you find the number to beat, with bare ears.

flow.do: Build the first design from card and tape. Test it with eyes closed. Write the distance where your child first hears the tick.
flow.say: Build your first design. Put it on, close your eyes, and say now when you hear the tick.
flow.kid: Build your first design. Test it with your eyes closed.

check.q: Which change would make a cone catch more sound?
options: A wider opening at the sound end
A smaller opening at the sound end
Facing the opening away from the sound
check.why: A wider opening collects sound from a bigger area, and the cone guides it to the ear. Facing away from the sound, or making the opening small, collects less.

flow.context: In this step, you build and test your first design.

flow.do: Change one thing, such as the size of the opening or the shape. Test again. Write the new distance. Do this once or twice more.
flow.say: Change just one thing. Test again. Did it help? Change only one thing at a time, so you know what made the difference.
flow.kid: Change one thing. Test again. Did it help?
flow.parent: Only one change at a time is the key idea. If your child changes two things at once, they will not know which one worked.
flow.context: In this step, you change one thing and test again.

flow.do: Compare all the distances. Ask your child which design worked best and why. Ask which animal's ears it is most like.
flow.say: Which design worked best? Why do you think so? Which animal's ears does it most look like?
flow.kid: Which design worked best? Why? Which animal is it like?
flow.think: What would you change to make your ears work even better?
flow.context: In this step, you compare designs and think about animal ears.

items.p: Which sense organ does a fish use to feel water moving along her sides?
items.why: The lateral line is a row of tiny sensors along a fish's sides. Hairs in it bend when water moves. An eardrum is for sound, a heat pit is for warmth, and an ear flap collects sound.

items.p: All animals with a backbone use exactly the same senses in exactly the same way.
items.why: False. All five groups have eyes, ears, a nose and touch, but each group has developed some of them much further. Fish have a lateral line, some snakes have heat pits, and many birds see ultraviolet.

items.p: A small hollow in a snake's face that feels the heat of a warm body is called a heat ____.
items.why: A heat pit has a thin skin inside that reacts to infrared, the heat given off by warm bodies. Pit vipers, boas and pythons have them.

items.p: Match each part to what it does.
pairs: feels the warmth of a body from a distance
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each sense organ picks up one kind of signal. The lateral line feels water movement, the heat pit feels infrared, the eardrum shakes with sound, and a cone reacts to colour.

items.p: Where does a frog's eardrum sit?
opts: Flat on the skin of her head, with no ear flap
Deep inside her head, behind an ear flap
At the end of her tail
items.why: A frog's eardrum is a round disc on the outside of her head, behind the eye. She has no ear flap. Mammals are the animals with ear flaps.

items.p: Sort each sense under the group that is best known for it.
items: a fourth colour cone for ultraviolet
items.a: as given
items.why: These are the best-known examples. Some of these senses are shared. Many fish and reptiles also see ultraviolet, for example. But the lateral line, the three middle-ear bones and the forked tongue are best known in the groups shown.

items.p: A dog sees only in black and white.
items.why: False. Dogs have two kinds of colour cones. They tell blue from yellow, but cannot tell red from green, like some people.

items.p: Why do many hunted animals, such as pigeons and horses, have eyes on the sides of the head?
opts: Side eyes give a very wide view, so they can spot a hunter from almost any side
Side eyes help to judge distance
Side eyes let them see in the dark
Side eyes make the head lighter
items.why: Eyes on the sides see a very wide view. But the two eyes share very little space, so judging distance is harder. Judging distance is what front eyes do best.

items.p: A pigeon sees about 340 degrees around her. A person sees about 200 degrees. How many more degrees does the pigeon see?
items.why: 340 take away 200 is 140. The pigeon sees 140 degrees more than a person.

items.p: Revathi says: 'A python in a dark storeroom sees a rat with her eyes.' Explain what is wrong with this idea.
items.a: A python does not need light. Her heat pits feel the warmth of the rat. So she can find the rat in the dark without seeing it.
items.why: A strong answer says that the python senses heat, not light, and names the heat pits. Saying 'she smells it' is partly true, since snakes smell with their tongues, but it leaves out the heat pits.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? Lateral line, heat pit, eardrum, claw.
items.a: The claw. The other three pick up a signal. A claw is for gripping or tearing.
items.why: A lateral line, a heat pit and an eardrum are sense organs that pick up water movement, heat and sound. A claw does not pick up a signal.

items.p: Put these in the right order for how a barn owl catches a rat in a dark room.
a: A rat rustles on the floor
The sound reaches the owl's face and ears
The owl turns her face towards the sound
The owl drops onto the spot
items.why: First the rat makes a sound. The owl's face gathers it, she turns until the sound is in front, and then she drops. She does not need light.

items.p: What does a small bat do to find a moth in the dark?
opts: Sends out high sounds and listens for the echoes
Smells the moth from far away
Feels the moth with her whiskers
Sees the moth in ultraviolet light
items.why: Echolocation means making a sound and listening to the echo that bounces back. The bat's calls are too high for people to hear.

items.p: Ears that stick out from the head and catch sound are called ear ____.
items.why: An ear flap, or pinna, collects sound and can often turn towards it. Mammals have ear flaps. Birds, frogs and snakes do not.

items.p: Draw a pond as a fish would sense it. Show where the lateral line is, and draw arrows for the ripples it feels.
items.a: A fish with a line along her side, and ripple lines reaching that line from an insect on the surface.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the lateral line along the side of the body, and ripple lines arriving at it from a falling insect.

items.p: A scientist wants to find out if a fish can feel ripples with her lateral line alone. Why should she make sure the fish cannot see or hear what makes the ripple?
items.a: If the fish could see or hear the ripple, she might turn because of that. The scientist needs to know that only the lateral line did it.
items.why: A fair test changes one thing and blocks other explanations. A strong answer says the fish might be using eyes or ears, and these must be ruled out.

items.p: Why might a male and a female bird that look alike to us look different to each other?
opts: Birds see ultraviolet, and their feathers may differ in ultraviolet
Birds have heat pits that show warmth
items.why: Most birds have a fourth kind of colour cone that senses ultraviolet. A feather can have a pattern in ultraviolet that people never see.

items.p: An owl cannot move her eyes in their sockets. How does she look to the side?
opts: She does not look to the side
items.why: An owl's eyes are fixed in tube-shaped sockets, so she turns her head instead, up to about 270 degrees.

items.p: Cobras find prey in the dark with heat pits.
items.why: False. Heat pits are found on pit vipers, boas and pythons. Cobras and Russell's vipers have none, so they use smell, touch and sight.

items.p: Sounds too low for people to hear are called ____.
items.why: Infrasound is sound below what people can hear. Asian elephants use it to call across a forest.

items.p: Put these in the right order for how a fish senses an insect that falls on the water.
a: An insect falls onto the water
The hairs of the lateral line bend
The fish turns towards the ripple
items.why: The fall makes ripples, the ripples move the water along the fish's side, the hairs bend and send a message, and the fish turns.

items.p: Sort each animal by the kind of eyes that help her most.
items.a: as given
items.why: Animals that are hunted, such as pigeons, horses and rabbits, tend to have side eyes for a wide view. Animals that hunt or leap, such as owls, cats and monkeys, tend to have front eyes for judging distance.

items.p: A fish lives in a dark cave and has no eyes. How might she still find food?
opts: Her lateral line and other senses work without light
She grows new eyes at night
Fish do not need to find food
items.why: Mexican cavefish have lost their eyes but have many more sensors on their lateral lines. Water movement tells them about food and walls.

items.p: A friend says: 'Bats are blind.' Give two pieces of evidence that this is wrong.
items.a: All bats can see. A large fruit bat such as the Indian flying fox finds ripe fruit with her eyes and nose. Small bats can also see, and they use echoes as well.
items.why: A strong answer says that bats can see, and gives an example such as the fruit bat. Echolocation is something extra that small bats use, and not a replacement for sight.

items.p: Match each animal to a signal she picks up that a person's body does not.
pairs: weak electricity from other animals' muscles
infrared heat from a warm body
echoes of sounds too high for people to hear
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: A shark finds hidden fish by electricity, a python by heat, a pigeon sees ultraviolet and a small bat uses high-pitched echoes.

items.p: Meera and Imran watch a python in a dark storeroom find a warm rat.

views.who: Meera, a girl in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: The storeroom is dark, so for the python the rat is hidden. She finds it only by luck.

views.who: Imran, a boy in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: The rat is not hidden to the python. She feels the rat's warmth, so the python lives in a different world from ours.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with more? What could you test to find out?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a side, gives a reason and names a test. For example, cover the python's eyes and see if she still strikes at a warm target but not a cool one.
items.why: Imran's view fits the evidence from snakes with covered eyes. A good test removes one sense at a time and checks the result.

items.p: According to most biologists, why does no animal have every sense?
opts: Senses cost energy, and each animal keeps the ones that fit her life
Nobody has looked for more senses
items.why: Eyes, ears and the brain parts that read them use a lot of energy. A sense that is hardly needed is a waste of food. This is a widely held idea, and scientists are still measuring the costs.

items.p: Scientists fully understand how birds sense the Earth's magnetic field.
items.why: False. Experiments show that birds use the magnetic field, but the receptor has not been found with certainty. There are two main ideas, one based on light and one based on iron.

items.p: Draw a top view of a pigeon and an owl. Shade how far round each one can see, and write the angle beside each shape.
items.a: A pigeon with a very wide shaded wedge of about 340 degrees, and an owl with a narrow wedge of about 110 degrees with a larger overlap in front.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the pigeon seeing almost all the way round, with a small overlap in front, and the owl seeing a narrow wedge that is mostly overlap.

items.p: A harbour seal follows the swirl a fish left in the water. Which part does she use?
items.why: A seal's whiskers have many nerves at the base. They feel the swirl left in the water by a swimming fish.

items.p: A full circle is 360 degrees. A pigeon sees about 340 degrees. How many degrees does she not see?
items.why: 360 take away 340 is 20. Only a small slice straight behind her is hidden.

items.p: A snake's forked tongue gathers tiny bits of ____ from the air and ground.
items.why: The tongue carries scent into two spots in the roof of the mouth. The snake does not sting with it.

items.p: A cat judges a jump onto a wall using both eyes. Explain how two eyes help her.
items.a: Each eye sees the wall from a slightly different place. Her brain compares the two pictures and works out how far away the wall is.
items.why: A strong answer says the two pictures are different, and the brain uses the difference to judge distance.

worksheets.title: Think like a scientist about animal senses (challenge)

items.p: Design a test to find out if a guppy can feel ripples without seeing them. Say what you would change, what you would keep the same and what you would measure.
items.a: Make ripples near the fish in a dark or covered tank, so she cannot see them. Change only the distance. Keep the size of the ripple the same. Count how often the fish turns towards it.
items.why: A strong answer changes one thing (such as distance), keeps the others the same, and measures something countable, such as the turns. It also removes sight as a clue.

items.p: A child is blindfolded and keeps both hands still in water. She says the side of a ripple correctly 9, 7 and 5 times out of 10 at 5, 10 and 20 centimetres. Guessing gives about 5. At how many centimetres is her score the same as guessing?
items.why: At 5 centimetres she is right 9 times and at 10 centimetres 7 times, both more than 5. At 20 centimetres she scores 5, the same as guessing, so her skin could not feel the ripple that far away.

items.p: A python in a dark storeroom has a warm rat on one side and a warm hot-water bottle on the other. What might she do?
opts: Strike at either, because both are warm
Strike only at the rat because she can see it
items.why: Heat pits sense warmth, not whether the warm thing is food. In the dark, either one can fool her. This is why the experiments with warm targets work.

items.p: Because dogs see fewer colours than people, dogs are worse at everything to do with seeing.
items.why: False. Dogs see fewer colours, but they notice movement well and are thought to see well in dim light. Each animal's eyes fit her way of life.

items.p: Match each animal to the clue that shows her senses fit her way of life.
pairs: a heart-shaped face that gathers sound
eyes on the sides of the head
eyes with no lens, and clicks that make echoes
ear flaps that turn towards a sound
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each sense fits a way of life. The owl hunts in the dark by sound, the pigeon needs a wide view, the susu lives in muddy water, and the cat hunts by hearing small sounds.

items.p: Why does a barn owl catch a rat more easily when the rat walks on dry leaves?
opts: Dry leaves rustle, so the sound is louder and easier to hear
Dry leaves help the owl to see
items.why: A louder, sharper sound is easier for the owl to locate. This is why a rat that freezes and stays quiet is safer.

items.p: Asha and Karthik are talking about a tick on a branch. The tick reacts only to sweat smell, to body warmth and to hairy skin.

views.who: Asha, a girl in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: A tick and a person live in different worlds, because they notice very different things.

views.who: Karthik, a boy in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: There is one world. The tick and the person each notice a small part of it.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with more? What would count as evidence?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a side and gives a reason. Asha's view is the idea of Jakob von Uexküll. Karthik's is a view held by many scientists today.
items.why: Both views fit the facts. They differ in what 'world' means. This is a real debate, and nobody has settled it.

items.p: Explain why a lateral line works well in water, but would be little use to a bird flying in air.
items.a: Water is thick and carries a push or ripple a long way, so hairs along the body bend. Air is thin, and a push from a moving animal fades fast, so there would be almost nothing to feel.
items.why: A strong answer says that water carries movement much better than air. It is also true that birds rely on sight and hearing instead.

items.p: Sort each of these by whether a person's body can sense it without a tool.
items: a ripple of water on the hand
the heat of a diya on the cheek
the weak electricity of another animal's muscles
items.a: as given
items.why: People feel ripples, warmth and smells. Ultraviolet, the electricity of muscles and a bat's clicks are outside what our bodies can sense, though instruments can detect them.

items.p: Seeing the same thing with two eyes at once is called ____ vision.
items.why: Binocular vision is two eyes seeing the same space. The brain compares the two pictures to judge distance.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? Pigeon, horse, rabbit, owl.
items.a: The owl. Her eyes face forwards and give a deep view. The others have side eyes and a wide view.
items.why: Pigeons, horses and rabbits are hunted and need a wide view. An owl hunts, and needs to judge distance.

items.p: Draw an owl's face from the front. Add arrows to show how the face works as a dish that gathers sound.
items.a: A heart-shaped face with arrows curving inwards from the sides towards the ears.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the flat face as a dish, with arrows of sound gathering into the ears.

items.p: A scientist covers a snake's eyes and nostrils. The snake still strikes at a warm target but not at a cool one. What does this show?
opts: The snake can sense heat, not just light or smell
items.why: With sight and smell blocked, the only difference left between the two targets is warmth. So the snake must sense warmth.

items.p: A farmer says: 'Owls bring bad luck.' Write one fair question you could ask, and one way to test it, to find out whether owls help or harm the farmer.
items.a: How many rats are in the granary with and without an owl? Count the rat holes in the sacks for two weeks with an owl, and then compare with two weeks without one.
items.why: A strong answer asks a question that can be tested and describes a fair comparison. It treats the farmer's belief with respect while looking for evidence.

items.p: A clock's tick is heard from 120 centimetres with bare ears, and from 150 centimetres with a card cone at one ear. By how many centimetres did the cone help?
items.why: 150 take away 120 is 30. The cone let the tick be heard from 30 centimetres farther away.

items.p: Ear flaps are found on mammals, and not on any bird, frog or snake.
items.why: True. The outer ear flap, or pinna, belongs to mammals. Birds, frogs and snakes have an eardrum or none, but no ear flap.

opts: Reacts to one kind of signal and sends a message
quiz.why: A receptor is a tiny cell that reacts to one kind of signal, such as light, a smell or a push, and sends a message to the brain.

quiz.p: Which animal feels moving water with a lateral line?
quiz.why: Fish have a lateral line. Cows and crows have no such sensors, and a python feels heat with her pits.

quiz.p: A python lies in the dark and finds a warm rat. Which part senses the rat?
opts: The heat pits on her lips
quiz.why: Pythons have heat pits along their lips. They sense the infrared given off by a warm body. Pythons have no ear flaps or whiskers.

quiz.p: Why does a pigeon see almost all the way round?
opts: Her eyes are on the sides of her head
Her eyes are at the front
Her eyes move around inside her head
quiz.why: Eyes on the sides of the head see a very wide view. This helps a hunted animal to spot danger from any side.

quiz.p: Why do owls and cats judge distance well?
opts: Their eyes face forwards and overlap
Their eyes are on the sides
quiz.why: When two eyes see the same space, the brain compares the pictures and works out distance. Side eyes overlap very little.

quiz.p: How does a cupped hand behind the ear help you hear?
opts: It catches more sound and guides it in
It makes the sound louder at the source
quiz.why: The hand works as a bigger ear flap. It collects more of the sound and points it into the ear.

quiz.p: How does a barn owl catch a rat in a dark room?
opts: She hears the rat and turns her face towards the sound
quiz.why: Barn owls can find a rat in complete darkness using sound alone. Her flat face works like a dish that gathers sound.

quiz.p: Dogs see only in black and white.
quiz.why: False. Dogs see blues and yellows, and cannot tell red from green.

quiz.p: Which group of animals with a backbone has three tiny bones in the middle ear?
quiz.why: Only mammals have three middle-ear bones. Birds and reptiles have one.

quiz.p: You test whether cupped hands help you hear a clock. What should stay the same in a fair test?
opts: The clock, the room and the way the helper walks
quiz.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. Here, only the position of the ears should change. Everything else, such as the clock, the room and the walking, stays the same.

quiz.p: Which of these do scientists still not fully understand?
opts: How birds sense the Earth's magnetic field
That fish have a lateral line
That snakes smell with their tongue
quiz.why: Birds seem to use the magnetic field, but the sensor has not been found with certainty. The other three are well shown.

quiz.p: Match each group to a sense that stands out in it.
pairs: ear flaps and three middle-ear bones
quiz.why: Each group is best known for these senses. Some are shared with other groups, but these are the clearest examples.

applications: Thermal cameras, used by firefighters to find people in smoke, do something like what a python's heat pits do.
Doctors use ultrasound scans of a baby before birth. The scan uses echoes, the way a bat does.
Ships measure the depth of the sea with sonar, which is echolocation by machine.
Sniffer dogs are trained to find lost people, and researchers are testing dogs for finding some illnesses.
Scientists record bat calls with special microphones to count bats without catching them.
Robots with whisker-like sensors can feel their way through dark places.
Designers shape hearing dishes and microphones like an owl's face or a fox's ear, to catch faint sounds.
Engineers copy the lateral line when they build sensors that feel water flow around a boat or under the sea.

open_questions.q: How exactly do birds sense the Earth's magnetic field?
open_questions.why_open: Experiments show that birds and some other animals use the field. But two ideas, one based on light and one on iron, are still debated, and the receptor has not been found with certainty.

open_questions.q: What does a heat pit feel like to a snake? Is it a kind of seeing, a kind of feeling, or something else?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can measure how the pit reacts and how the brain handles it. Nobody can tell what the snake experiences.

open_questions.q: How does a fish in a big school use her lateral line to swim so close to others without bumping?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have models and experiments, but they have not settled how much comes from the lateral line, how much from sight, and how much from simple rules.

open_questions.q: Are there senses that animals have, but that scientists have not found yet?
open_questions.why_open: New senses keep turning up. The heat pit and the electric sense were only found in the last two hundred years. Nobody knows how many more there are.

open_questions.q: How does an animal's brain decide which signals to pay attention to, and which to ignore?
open_questions.why_open: A body is flooded with signals. Scientists know that brains filter them, but they are still working out how.

open_questions.q: Can anyone know what it is like to be a bat?
open_questions.why_open: This is a question about experience, not measurement. The philosopher Thomas Nagel asked it in 1974, and it has not been settled.

maths.problem: A pigeon sees about 340 degrees, and a person about 200 degrees. An owl sees about 110 degrees. How many degrees more than the owl does a person see? How many more than a person does a pigeon see?
maths.answer: A person sees 90 degrees more than the owl. A pigeon sees 140 degrees more than a person.
maths.explain: 200 take away 110 is 90. 340 take away 200 is 140.
maths.context: In the Wide View, Deep View test, you measured how far round you could see and compared it with a pigeon and an owl.
maths.why_maths: Taking one angle from another tells you exactly how much wider one view is than another.

maths.problem: A full circle is 360 degrees. A pigeon sees about 340 degrees. What fraction of the full circle can the pigeon see? Write it as simply as you can.
maths.explain: The pigeon sees 340 out of 360. Divide both numbers by 20. 340 divided by 20 is 17, and 360 divided by 20 is 18. So she sees 17 eighteenths of the circle.
maths.why_maths: A fraction shows how much of the whole circle an animal sees, so views of different animals can be compared.

maths.problem: In the Cup Your Ears test, a child hears a tick from 120 centimetres with bare ears, and from 160 centimetres with cupped hands. By what fraction of 120 centimetres did the cupped hands help?
maths.explain: 160 take away 120 is 40. 40 out of 120 is 1 out of 3, because 120 divided by 40 is 3. So the cupped hands added a third.
maths.context: In the Cup Your Ears test, a ticking clock was moved closer until your child first heard it.
maths.why_maths: A fraction shows how big the help was compared with where you started, so it can be compared with other tests.

maths.problem: In the Ripple Skin test, a coin toss decides left or right. If a child guesses every time, how many answers do you expect to be right out of 10? Out of 30? A child gets 9 right out of 10 at one distance. Is that likely to happen by guessing alone?
maths.answer: About 5 out of 10, and about 15 out of 30. Getting 9 out of 10 by guessing would happen only about 1 time in 100.
maths.explain: A coin lands left half the time, so a guess is right half the time. Half of 10 is 5, and half of 30 is 15. Getting 9 or 10 right out of 10 by luck happens in about 11 of every 1,024 tries, which is about 1 in 100. So 9 out of 10 is strong evidence that the child really felt the ripple.
maths.context: In the Ripple Skin test, you tossed a coin to choose the side of each ripple, and the child said left or right.
maths.why_maths: Knowing what pure guessing gives tells you whether a score shows real sensing or just luck.

maths.problem: About how many species are known in each group? Fish 36,000. Reptiles 12,000. Birds 11,000. Amphibians 8,700. Mammals 6,500. These are rough numbers. About how many times as many species of fish are there as mammals?
maths.explain: 36,000 divided by 6,500 is a little more than 5. Five times 6,500 is 32,500, and 6 times is 39,000. So the answer is between 5 and 6, close to 5 and a half.
maths.why_maths: A comparison like this shows which group is biggest, and so which senses are found in most animals with a backbone.

maths.problem: An owl turns her head about 270 degrees. A right angle is 90 degrees. How many right angles is that? What fraction of a full turn?
maths.answer: 3 right angles, which is three quarters of a full turn.
maths.explain: 270 divided by 90 is 3. A full turn is 360 degrees, or 4 right angles. So 3 out of 4 right angles is three quarters.
maths.why_maths: Counting right angles is a quick way to describe how far a head, a hand or a door turns.

maths.problem: A bat sends out a call and hears the echo 0.01 seconds later. Sound travels about 340 metres in 1 second. About how far away is the moth?
maths.explain: In 0.01 seconds, sound travels 340 times 0.01, which is 3.4 metres. That is the way there and back. So the moth is half of that away, which is 1.7 metres.
maths.why_maths: Decimals let you work out the tiny times and distances an echo uses, and show how a bat can judge distance by timing.

maths.problem: Suppose a small bat catches 600 insects in a night. This is a made-up number for practice. About how many does she catch in a week of 7 nights? In 30 nights?
maths.answer: About 4,200 in a week, and about 18,000 in 30 nights.
maths.explain: 600 times 7 is 4,200. 600 times 30 is 18,000. This is a made-up number, because real bats catch different amounts each night.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying a small number by many nights shows how much a bat's senses are worth over time.

playtest: Read as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, but not yet tried at home. Wide View, Deep View: the clock circle needs a clear floor of about 3 metres, and most people first see the moving card around 3 or 4 on the clock. With the right eye covered the card appears later, because the nose gets in the way. Pen touch scores depend on the child, so the steps say to write what you get. The pen must be capped. Ripple Skin: the basin should be at least 60 centimetres long (or use 5, 10 and 15 centimetres in a smaller one), the water still before every ripple, and the ears covered, or the splash sound gives the answer away. A score near 5 out of 10 at 20 centimetres is a real result and not a failure. Cup Your Ears: needs a quiet room and a soft tick, and the clock volume must be turned down so that it is only just audible at 1 metre. Warm Spot Finder: the adult checks the water first, and it must feel comfortably hot and never scalding, and the pots stay at least 2 centimetres from the skin, so warmth is usually felt only within a few centimetres. Nose Trail: use only safe, mild smells, with the room aired. Window Watch needs a window, balcony or terrace where birds come, so it is outside the core path. Whose World? has 24 cards and the back of each begins with all the groups that fit, so more than one token can score. Facts to check before the unit goes live: the field of view figures for the pigeon (about 340 degrees), person (about 200) and owl (about 110), which vary by source and method; the 2005 Eaton ultraviolet finding; the Newman and Hartline snake experiments; the year and place of Katy Payne's first elephant observations (1984, Portland, Oregon); the Indian rock python lip pits and the absence of pits in cobras; that dogs have many tens of times more smell receptors than people; the 2015 cavefish energy study; and the three videos, which have no address yet.
